title: F5 appoints Cathy Peterman as Chief People Officer
summary: Peterman will lead F5’s global people strategy, driving talent development, organizational design, and culture as the company continues to evolve and strengthen its leadership position in AI and cybersecurity.
body_text: SEATTLE – F5 (NASDAQ: FFIV), the global leader in delivering and securing every app and API, today announced the appointment of Cathy Peterman as Executive Vice President and Chief People Officer. Peterman joins F5’s executive leadership team reporting to Chairman, President and CEO, François Locoh-Donou. In this role, she will lead F5’s global people strategy, driving talent development, organizational design, and culture as the company continues to evolve and strengthen its leadership position in AI and cybersecurity. “Cathy brings a rare combination of strategic depth and genuine humanity that will raise the bar for how we invest in our people,” said Locoh-Donou. “She and I share a reverence for culture and its impact on driving sustained results. That shared vision will be key as we seize the opportunity in front of us, both in how we work and how we serve our customers.” Peterman brings 20 years of experience scaling complex technology organizations and guiding enterprises through transformative change. She joins F5 from Wayfair, where she served as Chief People Officer for the company’s technology organization. Additionally, she drove AI transformation and talent development for all 11,000 of the company’s global employees. Prior to Wayfair, Peterman spent six years at Amazon driving talent strategy across three distinct businesses supporting more than 40,000 employees. She held HR leadership roles spanning Amazon Advertising, Amazon Devices, Prime Video & Studios, and Physical Stores. Her expertise spans enterprise talent development, organizational design, executive compensation strategy, and leveraging AI to accelerate both operational efficiency and human potential. Throughout her career, she has designed and executed large-scale workforce transformations, M&A integrations, and global expansion strategies. “From my very first conversations, I recognized a company that treats talent and culture as a core strategy rather than a support function,” said Peterman. “It’s rare to find a mature technology company that has continually evolved while maintaining a fierce commitment to putting people first. It’s that powerful combination of growth ambition and human-first leadership that has me thrilled to join this exceptional team and partner with all F5ers to create an environment where everyone can do the best work of their career.” Peterman holds a BA from Villanova University and an MA from the University of Denver. She is based in Seattle, F5’s corporate headquarters. About F5 F5, Inc. (NASDAQ: FFIV) is the global leader that delivers and secures every app. Backed by three decades of expertise, F5 has built the industry’s premier platform—F5 Application Delivery and Security Platform (ADSP)—to deliver and secure every app, every API, anywhere: on-premises, in the cloud, at the edge, and across hybrid, multicloud environments. F5 is committed to innovating and partnering with the world’s largest and most advanced organizations to deliver fast, available, and secure digital experiences. Together, we help each other thrive and bring a better digital world to life. title: FINNY named a Top 50 Firm to Work for in WealthTech
summary: Search Chain Partners has named FINNY one of the Top 50 Firms to Work for in WealthTech, and we’re grateful to be included alongside some of the biggest names in fintech.
body_text: Search Chain Partners has named FINNY one of the Top 50 Firms to Work for in WealthTech, and we’re grateful to be included alongside some of the biggest names in fintech. This particular list is meaningful because instead of reviewing applications, it is self-sourced and relies on actual reputational analysis from months of conversations with founders, investors, and operators across the industry. Having our name included on open-ended questions about best places to work is a testament to everything we’ve done to build a culture that is collaborative, innovative, and most importantly, effective. The company is the team Product is no longer the moat it used to be. As AI allows faster-than-ever product and feature releases, any competitive advantage in the current release is ethereal. But improvements don’t happen on their own. The new moat is the quality of the team and the velocity at which we’re able to operate, iterate, and serve the needs of clients. The visceral drive to become the default growth solution for financial advisors is FINNY. We are proud of where our product is and what we’ve built so far, but far prouder of having a team and environment that will make the next version even better. Good people want to work with good people, so we’ve built an elite team from across the globe, including top talent from the US, Canada, Europe, Africa, and Asia. Joe Ortiz, our Head of People & Talent, noted that “we’ve built a team around a common spark - a need to innovate, improve, and serve. That’s led us to great hires who can mesh together seamlessly.” The office and perks are also awesome FINNY started in a Manhattan apartment, the east coast equivalent of the Silicon Valley garage. Once we outgrew that space, the next obvious step was to find a home that matched the relentless and innovative culture of the team, which ended up being a former artist’s loft in Chelsea. We also make sure that everyone can keep their focus on their work, by offering great pay, real equity, benefits worth having, and a level of trust that lets people actually take their PTO. We took the whole company to Canada for an offsite, held Knicks watch parties during the playoffs, have frequent happy hours, and hold a weekly company soccer game. Taking time to really bond makes us stronger, and enables us to go farther together than any of us could alone. Back to growth We don’t spend significant time chasing list inclusions or awards; we’re too focused on building great solutions for financial advisors, and we have some huge projects in the works. As an organization dedicated to helping our clients grow, we can’t skip a beat. Consider this a quick bow, and now we’re already focused on what’s next. Congratulations to the other 49 firms on the list - we’re happy to be in your company.

title: Accelerating Product and Platform Innovations Across Coursera and Udemy
summary: New AI-powered experiences, accessibility enhancements, and enterprise tools to better serve our global community of learners and customers Since our recent closing of the Coursera and Udemy combination, we’ve been focused on one priority: delivering more value for learners, partners, and customers. By bringing together our teams and expertise, we’re able to move faster and introduce new […]
body_text: Accelerating Product and Platform Innovations Across Coursera and Udemy July 10, 2026 By Patrick Supanc Udemy News New AI-powered experiences, accessibility enhancements, and enterprise tools to better serve our global community of learners and customers Since our recent closing of the Coursera and Udemy combination, we’ve been focused on one priority: delivering more value for learners, partners, and customers. By bringing together our teams and expertise, we’re able to move faster and introduce new experiences that help learners build in-demand skills and organizations achieve better outcomes. I’m excited to share several new capabilities across Coursera and Udemy, from AI-powered learning experiences and accessibility enhancements to enterprise tools that help organizations build and measure workforce skills more effectively. Helping Learners Build and Demonstrate Skills with AI AI is creating new opportunities for learners to practice and validate skills in real world environments, helping learners move beyond content consumption to hands-on skill development. Graded Labs and Role Play (Coursera): We launched a pilot that turns hands-on labs and Role Play activities into graded assessments with AI-powered evaluation, giving learners trusted evidence of their applied skills while helping employers and educators better verify job readiness. Expanded Cloud Labs (Udemy): We expanded in-course labs with new AWS, AWS Bedrock, Azure, and Azure OpenAI workspaces, making it easier for instructors to create hands-on learning experiences with the cloud technologies learners use on the job. Next Best Recommendations (Coursera): A new personalized recommendation experience helps learners discover relevant content after completing a course or Specialization, making it easier to continue building skills and earn valuable credentials. Next Best Recommendation Creating More Personalized and Accessible Learning Experiences Learning works best when it adapts to individual preferences and helps learners maintain momentum. These recent enhancements make it easier for learners to engage with content in the ways that work best for them. Enhanced Role Play (Udemy): New customization and video capabilities give organizations greater flexibility to tailor role play experiences to specific learning objectives and workplace scenarios. Voice Enhancements (Coursera): Learners can now use their voice across AI-powered learning experiences, including speaking directly with AI personas in Role Play activities and responding verbally in Dialogue through new speech-to-text capabilities. These enhancements create more natural and immersive ways to deepen understanding and build workplace skills. Dark Mode on Web (Coursera): One of our most requested learner features is now available across desktop and mobile web, creating a more consistent experience across devices while supporting learner comfort and accessibility. Audio Mode for Readings (Coursera): Learners can now listen to a selection of reading content through a new read-aloud experience that automatically advances through course materials. Giving Learning Leaders Better Insights and Support Organizations increasingly need tools that help them understand program performance, support learners, and demonstrate business impact. This quarter, we introduced new capabilities designed specifically for enterprise administrators. Expanded Team Plan Upskilling Tools (Udemy Business): Team Plan customers can now create AI-generated Learning Paths, assign courses, paths, and assessments, and access more than 500 skill assessments to benchmark proficiency and track learner progress—bringing structured upskilling and skills measurement to organizations of all sizes. Team Plan Learning Paths Skills Intelligence Foundation (Udemy): We expanded Udemy’s Skills Library, a standardized skills taxonomy that helps connect content and learning activities to measurable skills. This foundation supports more personalized, skills-based learning experiences and lays the groundwork for richer skills insights across the platform. Expanded Enterprise Integrations (Coursera + Udemy): We expanded integrations with Workday and Degreed, making it easier to surface personalized learning within the enterprise tools employees already use. These updates improve content discovery, streamline administration, and help organizations connect learning to workforce skills and outcomes. Enterprise MCP Capabilities (Coursera + Udemy): We expanded our Model Context Protocol (MCP) capabilities, giving organizations a secure, standardized way to connect AI tools — including their own assistants and agents — to Coursera and Udemy learning experiences. Learners can discover relevant content, personalized learning paths, and skill-building resources directly within AI-powered workflows. Enhanced Admin Experience (Coursera): The new Admin Home has been redesigned with a unified dashboard for utilization, engagement, and skills insights, alongside Admin AI , a pilot for select enterprise administrators that uses conversational AI to turn learning data into actionable insights, helping organizations better understand program performance and impact. Admin AI AI innovations continue to create new opportunities to help people build skills, advance careers, and adapt to change. These recent updates reflect the broader direction we’re pursuing across Coursera and Udemy: making learning more personalized, more adaptive, and more connected to real-world outcomes. Previous Coursera and Udemy are now one company, creating the world’s most comprehensive skills platform

Fiscal Third Quarter 2026 Infor matio n Won 31 manufacturing programs during the quarter representing $255 million in annualized revenue when fully ramped into production. Purchased $20.6 million of our shares at an average price of $258.75 per share under our 2026 Share Repurchase Program, leaving $21.4 million available under our existing $100.0 million authorization. Todd Kelsey, President and Chief Executive Officer, commented, “Plexus generated record quarterly revenue in the fiscal third quarter by capturing strengthening end market demand and successfully launching numerous new programs. Fiscal third quarter revenue of $1.305 billion exceeded guidance, increasing 12% sequentially and 28% year over year. In addition, non-GAAP operating margin of 6.3% met the high end of guidance, non-GAAP EPS of $2.32 exceeded guidance and we again delivered healthy working capital efficiency.” Mr. Kelsey added, “Our go-to-market team continued to drive strong performance with quarterly manufacturing wins of $255 million in annualized revenue. This result included significant wins for our Aerospace/Defense market sector as well as a new partnership in our Industrial market sector manufacturing a battery energy storage system for data centers. Furthermore, we expanded our funnel of qualified manufacturing opportunities to $4.5 billion, a record level, supporting the potential to sustain robust long-term revenue growth.” David Abuhl, Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, commented, “Driven by continued progress on our working capital initiatives, our cash cycle of 62 days exceeded expectations. This outstanding result is the best quarterly cash cycle performance in over five years. In support of accelerating revenue growth, we had a slight usage of free cash flow in the quarter, which was better than our expectations. While we expect to maintain cash cycle days in the low-to-mid 60s for the fiscal fourth quarter, further working capital investments are required to support our substantial revenue growth projections. As such, we now expect a usage of free cash flow for fiscal 2026 with a return to meaningful free cash flow generation in early fiscal 2027.” Mr. Abuhl continued, “Our favorable cash cycle days, prudent capital expenditures and strong operating performance produced a return on invested capital of 14.9% in the quarter, up 110 basis points versus the prior quarter and 590 basis points above our cost of capital. This result represented the highest return in nearly five years.” Mr. Kelsey continued, “For our fiscal fourth quarter, we forecast continued revenue growth led by strength in our Healthcare/Life Sciences and Industrial market sectors, including our semiconductor capital equipment subsector. We are guiding revenue of $1.330 to $1.380 billion, up 4% sequentially and 28% year over year at the midpoint, non-GAAP operating margin of 6.1% to 6.5% and non-GAAP EPS of $2.47 to $2.63. For fiscal 2026, we now anticipate generating in excess of 20% revenue growth due to Plexus’ success in launching numerous new programs and our market share gains combined with improved end market demand. Additionally, we expect to deliver this considerable revenue growth with greater than 6% non-GAAP operating margin and healthy working capital efficiency.” Mr. Kelsey concluded, “Our differentiated value proposition, focused on providing unmatched quality and delivery, is resulting in robust performance for fiscal 2026 and positions Plexus for sustained, long-term momentum. We currently see the potential to generate fiscal 2027 revenue growth in excess of our 9% to 12% goal led by our Aerospace/Defense and Industrial market sectors, including our semiconductor capital equipment subsector. In addition, we anticipate delivering operating margin expansion, while continuing to make important investments in talent and technology in support of future growth.” Quarterly Comparison Three Months Ended (in thousands, except EPS) July 4, 2026 Apr 4, 2026 Jun 28, 2025 Revenue $ 1,304,778 $ 1,163,757 $ 1,018,308 Gross profit 131,379 119,176 103,288 Operating income 61,260 61,837 53,608 Net income 42,993 49,809 45,116 Diluted EPS $ 1.58 $ 1.82 $ 1.64 Gross margin 10.1 % 10.2 % 10.1 % Operating margin 4.7 % 5.3 % 5.3 % ROIC (1) 14.9 % 13.8 % 14.1 % Economic return (1) 5.9 % 4.8 % 5.2 % (1) Refer to Non-GAAP Supplemental Information tables for non-GAAP financial measures discussed and/or disclosed in this release, such as adjusted operating margin, adjusted net income, adjusted diluted EPS, ROIC and economic return. Plexus defines ROIC as tax-effected annualized adjusted operating income divided by average invested capital over a four-quarter period for the third fiscal quarter. Invested capital is defined as equity plus debt and operating lease obligations, less cash and cash equivalents. Plexus' weighted average cost of capital for fiscal 2026 is 9.0%. ROIC for the third quarter of fiscal 2026 less Plexus’ weighted average cost of capital resulted in an economic return of 5.9%. Free Cash Flow Plexus defines free cash flow as cash flows provided by operations less capital expenditures. title: 9 Tips to Increase Your Score | Northwest Bank
summary: Don’t let misconceptions and outdated advice get in the way of steps that can help. Instead, follow these nine tips to help improve your credit score over time.
body_text: Education | July 03, 2026 Your Credit Score Isn’t Stuck: 9 Tips to Increase Your Score Key Takeaways: Paying bills on time and keeping credit utilization low can have the biggest impact on your credit score. Regularly checking your credit score can help you track progress and catch errors without hurting your score. Small actions like paying down balances and limiting new credit inquiries can help strengthen your credit over time. While an impressive 83% of Americans say they’re prioritizing maintaining or improving their credit score this year, a recent FICO study shows a knowledge gap about what consumers think impacts their credit score. For instance, nearly t hree-quarters of consumers believe that carrying small balances on credit cards positively affects their score. That’s a misconception that could lead you to pay more interest and underutilize your credit. Meanwhile, one in five consumers mistakenly believe that checking their score will lower it. Don’t let misconceptions and outdated advice get in the way of steps that can help. Instead, follow these nine tips to help improve your credit score over time. 1. Check your credit score regularly The good news is that checking your credit score won’t negatively impact it. What’s more, by regularly checking your credit score and report, you can catch errors, make plans for improvement, and see your progress in real time. Our Credit Score tool lets you see your score right away and offers tips to help improve it. You can also go to annualcreditreport.com to access free credit reports from the three credit reporting companies: TransUnion, Experian and Equifax. Stagger your requests across agencies so you can view a new one every few months. If you spot an error, report it to the credit bureau that listed it so your score isn’t affected by incorrect information . 2. Automate your monthly payments Payment history accounts for 35% of your overall credit score. That's why it's important to pay your credit card minimum payments, installment loan payments and other monthly obligations on time. You can use digital banking tools, such as B ill Pay , to automate your payments and ensure they arrive on time. An account sent to collections can stay on your credit report for up to seven years. Prioritize on-time payments, and if you’ve been late in the past, you can rebuild your score with consistent, automated payments. 3. Keep your credit utilization below 10% Your credit utilization ratio accounts for 30% of your credit score. It’s the sum of the balances you carry on all your revolving credit accounts, expressed as a percentage of the total available credit. In a simple example, if you have a $3,000 balance on a credit card with a $10,000 limit, your utilization ratio is 30%. While experts recommend keeping your credit utilization below 30%, lowering it to 10% or less can boost your credit score. 4. Leave older credit accounts open Some people assume that closing old credit cards will improve their credit score. While it’s a good idea if you’re trying to reduce the temptation to spend, keeping them open can actually benefit your score more. The unused available credit can help reduce your overall utilization ratio. The credit reporting companies also consider the average age of accounts when creating your score, so having an older, unused account can work to your advantage. 5. Ask credit issuers to increase your limit In a similar strategy, you can ask your current credit card companies to increase the limit on your account. While you still want to focus on paying down your balances, boosting the amount of credit available can help enhance your credit score. However, keep in mind that this strategy only works if the available credit remains unused. 6. Use rent reporting services In the past, landlords usually haven't reported rent payments to credit bureaus. However, for many borrowers, especially those in the early stages of their financial lives, rent and utilities account for a significant share of their payment history. Check out services such as Experian Boost , which connects to your bank account and scans for recurring monthly payments to add to your credit report — so your score better reflects your rental payment history. 7. Become an authorized user If you’re a younger borrower or have a shorter credit history, consider asking a relative or trusted friend with excellent credit to add you to their older credit accounts. In doing so, you’ll instantly increase the average age of your own credit accounts and decrease your credit utilization, both of which can help increase your credit score. However, you need to be sure that the person you choose has healthy financial habits; if they run up their balances or miss minimum payments, that can affect your score as well. 8. Pay down balances Prioritize paying down your credit card balances as fast as possible. You can make more than one payment per month, if that's possible, and you can pay far more than the minimum balance. By paying down your debt, you’ll not only avoid paying the high interest associated with credit cards, but you’ll also improve your credit utilization ratio, which can increase your credit score. 9. Limit new credit inquiries New credit applications result in a hard inquiry to your credit report, which can temporarily diminish your credit score. Try to only apply for credit when you truly need it. If you’re seeking an installment loan, try to make inquiries to lenders in a short time period. The credit bureaus won’t ding your credit score for rate shopping , as long as the hard inquiries are within the same time span and for the same loan type. When it comes to your credit score, knowledge is power. Use these tips to steadily build your credit score and improve your financial well-being in the process. Enroll in Northwest’s free credit monitoring tool, Credit Score , in online and mobile banking to keep track of your credit . title: Prototype to Production Guide: Hardware, AI & Product Launch
summary: Learn how to move from prototype to production, from product validation and hardware manufacturing to AI deployment, quality control, compliance, monitoring, and launch.
body_text: Moving from prototype to production is the moment where an idea has to become reliable, usable, and scalable. For a hardware product, that can mean moving from a 3D-printed prototype to low-volume manufacturing, compliance testing, quality control, and full production. For an AI product, it can mean moving from a working model or prompt chain to a monitored, governed, production-ready system. But many products also need something else before they are ready for real users: an application layer. That app layer might be a dashboard for customers, a portal for pilot users, an internal tool for operations, a device management interface, an AI review workflow, or an admin panel for support. Without it, the prototype may work technically, but users still do not have a reliable way to interact with the product. This guide explains the prototype-to-production journey for hardware and AI products, and where builders can use tools like WeWeb to create the apps, dashboards, and workflows that help turn a prototype into something people can actually use. Understanding the Early Stages Before you can think about mass production, you need a solid foundation. The initial phases are all about validating your idea and ensuring you’re building something people actually want. Market Research and Product Market Fit Market research is the process of gathering information about your target customers, competitors, and the overall market landscape. The goal is to find product market fit, which means your product perfectly meets a real market need that customers are willing to pay for. This isn’t just a good idea; it’s critical for survival. A staggering 35% of launched products fail to deliver a significant return on investment, often due to a lack of market need. Skipping this step is like setting sail without a map. You need to confirm you’re solving a genuine problem before you invest significant time and money. Early Stage Prototyping and Validation Once you have an idea validated by research, the next step is early stage prototyping. This involves creating preliminary versions of your product to test your concept. A prototype can be a simple 3D print, a clickable software wireframe, or a functional web app. The purpose is to learn quickly and cheaply. Getting a prototype in front of users provides invaluable feedback. In fact, testing a prototype with just five target users can uncover about 85% of usability issues. This iterative process of building, testing, and learning significantly reduces risk. Need expert help accelerating your MVP? Browse our agency directory . Modern tools have made this faster than ever. For instance, some companies have cut development time by up to 90% using no code prototyping tools . Platforms like WeWeb allow founders to build and test a functional web app MVP in days, accelerating the journey from a rough idea to a validated concept. Navigating the Physical Product Lifecycle For physical products, the path from prototype to production involves careful planning around design, manufacturing, and logistics. This entire process is often called the new product introduction (NPI) lifecycle. The Prototype to Production Lifecycle The prototype to production lifecycle covers every stage from the initial concept to a mass produced product available for sale. Poor management of this process is a primary reason for failure. About 46% of resources spent on new products are wasted on items that never launch or fail in the market. A well managed lifecycle includes phases like concept validation, design for manufacturability, and pilot production runs to ensure a smooth transition. Design for Manufacturability (DFM) Design for Manufacturability (DFM) is an engineering philosophy focused on designing products that are easy and cost effective to produce at scale. The decisions made during the design phase determine roughly 70 to 80% of a product’s final manufacturing cost. DFM involves simplifying geometry, standardizing parts, and selecting materials that are easy to work with. Involving manufacturing partners early in this stage can prevent expensive redesigns down the road. Bill of Materials (BOM) A Bill of Materials (BOM) is the complete recipe for your product. It’s a detailed list of every single part, component, and raw material required for assembly, along with the specific quantities. For a complex product like a car, the BOM can include around 30,000 individual components. An accurate BOM is essential for procurement, assembly, and cost calculation. Any error in the BOM can halt production, leading to costly delays. Manufacturing Partner Selection Choosing the right manufacturing partner is one of the most critical decisions you’ll make. This partner, or contract manufacturer, will be responsible for turning your design into a physical reality. You need to evaluate potential partners on their capabilities, capacity, cost, and quality standards. A good partner acts as an extension of your team, providing valuable feedback and ensuring a smooth production process. A poor choice can lead to delays, quality issues, and budget overruns. Tooling Selection and Optimization Tooling refers to the specialized equipment, molds, dies, and fixtures needed to manufacture your product’s components. This often represents a major upfront investment. A single high precision steel injection mold can cost anywhere from $10,000 to over $100,000. Optimizing your tooling, for example by using modular designs or advanced cooling techniques, can dramatically improve production efficiency and lower your per unit cost. For instance, using 3D printed conformal cooling channels in a mold can cut cycle times by 20 to 40%. Mold Strategy and Cavity Planning For plastic parts, mold strategy and cavity planning are key. This involves deciding on the number of cavities (the part shapes) within a mold. A single cavity mold is cheaper upfront and ideal for initial runs, while a multi cavity mold produces more parts per cycle, lowering the unit cost for high volume production. A common strategy is to start with a single cavity mold for early validation and then invest in a multi cavity mold once the design is finalized and demand is proven. Low Volume Manufacturing (Bridge Production) Low volume manufacturing, also known as bridge production, is an intermediate step between prototyping and full scale mass production. It involves producing a small batch of units, perhaps a few hundred to a few thousand. This allows you to get products to early adopters, validate your manufacturing process, and gather real world feedback before committing to a massive production run. This approach serves as a valuable insurance policy, helping you ensure that when you scale, you get it right the first time. Digital Tools Hardware Builders Need Before Launch A hardware product often needs more than the physical device. As you move toward production, you may need internal and customer-facing tools around the product. Examples include: Pilot user portal: Let early customers register devices, submit feedback, report issues, and access setup instructions. Device management dashboard: View device status, usage data, error logs, firmware versions, and customer accounts. Manufacturing tracker: Track batches, suppliers, test results, defects, and production milestones. Quality control app: Record inspections, flag issues, upload photos, and document test results. Support admin panel: Help support teams view customer devices, troubleshoot problems, and manage replacements. Customer onboarding flow: Guide users through setup, account creation, configuration, and product activation. Post-launch analytics dashboard: Track adoption, usage, failures, returns, and product feedback. These tools do not replace manufacturing, compliance, or quality systems. But they can make the product easier to operate, support, and improve once real users are involved. With WeWeb, builders can create these dashboards, portals, and internal tools visually while connecting to device data, backend workflows, APIs, and databases. Pre compliance Testing and Certification Before you can sell your product, it must meet various regulatory standards for safety, emissions, and more (like FCC, UL, or CE certifications). Pre compliance testing is a dress rehearsal for the official certification process. It involves testing your product in house or with a third party lab to catch and fix any issues early. Failing an official compliance test can cause major delays and require expensive redesigns, so this proactive step is essential for de risking your launch. Ensuring Quality and Efficiency Once production begins, the focus shifts to maintaining quality, optimizing processes, and managing the complexities of the supply chain. Design and Process Optimization This is the practice of continuously improving both the product design and the manufacturing processes. Optimization can involve refining the design to use fewer parts, streamlining production steps, or implementing methodologies like Lean and Six Sigma to eliminate waste. The impact can be enormous. For example, Motorola reported saving more than $16 billion over two decades as a result of its Six Sigma quality and process improvement efforts. Quality Control and Documentation Quality Control (QC) is the system of inspecting products and processes to ensure they meet defined standards. Good documentation, including assembly instructions and test results, is the backbone of effective QC. It’s far cheaper to catch a defect early. The cost to fix an error rises exponentially the later it’s found in the process. A defect found in the design phase might cost $1 to fix, but that same defect could cost $100 to fix once the product is in a customer’s hands. The Right First Time Quality Approach The “Right First Time” philosophy aims to perform every step of a process correctly on the first attempt, eliminating rework. This is often measured by First Pass Yield, the percentage of products made without any defects. This approach, championed by quality expert Philip Crosby, is based on the idea that “Quality is Free” because the savings from preventing failures far outweigh the investment in better processes. Supply Chain Planning and Risk Mitigation Supply chain planning involves organizing the flow of materials from suppliers to your factory and finally to your customers. Risk mitigation means identifying potential disruptions, such as material shortages or logistics delays, and creating backup plans. The global semiconductor chip shortage, which cost the auto industry an estimated $210 billion in lost revenue in 2021, is a stark reminder of why a resilient supply chain is so important. Strategies like having multiple suppliers for critical components can prevent costly shutdowns. Transition to Serial Production The transition to serial production is when you move from making small batches to continuous, high volume manufacturing. This is where the rubber meets the road. This phase involves setting up dedicated assembly lines, validating processes at scale, and ramping up production volume gradually. This is often where hidden problems are exposed, as famously described by Elon Musk as “production hell” during the Tesla Model 3 ramp up. Careful planning is key to a smooth transition. Product Launch and Post Launch Evaluation The product launch is when your product officially becomes available to customers. But the work doesn’t stop there. Post launch evaluation is the critical process of gathering data on sales, customer feedback, and product performance. Instrument your app to track key events with Google Tag Manager so you can iterate quickly. This feedback loop is vital for making necessary adjustments and informing the development of future products. It turns the launch from a single event into a cycle of planning, executing, measuring, and learning. The Journey from Prototype to Production in AI The prototype to production lifecycle isn’t limited to hardware. Developing and deploying AI models follows a similar, though distinct, path. Platform and Model Selection (Generative AI) For a generative AI project, the first step is choosing the right AI model and platform. This means deciding between large, powerful models like OpenAI’s GPT series or smaller, open source alternatives like Meta’s LLaMA 2. You also have to choose how to access it, whether through a cloud API or by hosting it yourself. Using an API is convenient, but hosting your own model provides more control and can be more cost effective at scale. Building an application on a flexible platform like WeWeb allows you to easily integrate with various AI models via API , letting you experiment to find the perfect fit. Model Customization and Augmentation Off the shelf AI models are powerful, but they often need to be customized to perform well on specific tasks. Key techniques include: Prompt Optimization : Carefully crafting the input (the prompt) to guide the model toward the best possible output. Fine Tuning : Further training a pre trained model on your own dataset to specialize its knowledge and style. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) : Connecting the model to an external knowledge base to provide it with up to date, factual information (for example, pulling context from Airtable ) which helps reduce inaccuracies. Model Evaluation, KPI, and Monitoring Evaluating an AI model means measuring its performance using relevant Key Performance Indicators (KPIs). For generative AI, this can involve both automated metrics and human evaluation. After deployment, continuous monitoring is crucial to track performance and detect any degradation over time. A startling number of data science projects, potentially between 60% and 87%, never deliver their intended value, often due to a lack of meaningful monitoring after launch. Responsible AI Governance and Safety Responsible AI governance involves creating frameworks to ensure AI systems are developed and used ethically, transparently, and safely. This includes auditing for bias, ensuring privacy, and building in safeguards to prevent harmful outputs. The infamous case of Microsoft’s Tay chatbot, which was taught to post offensive tweets within hours of its launch, serves as a powerful lesson in the importance of AI safety. Release, Validation, and Deployment The final stage is deploying the model into a live production environment. Unfortunately, many AI models never reach this stage. Some estimates suggest that over 80% of AI models developed in labs are never put into production. A successful deployment involves a careful release process, validation on real world data (often through A/B testing), and a scalable deployment infrastructure. This is the critical “last mile” that turns a promising AI prototype into a valuable production system. Ready to accelerate your own journey from prototype to production? Discover how WeWeb’s visual development platform can help you build and launch your application faster. See real‑world apps built with WeWeb for inspiration. Build the App Layer Btween Prototype and Production With WeWeb The journey from prototype to production is not only about manufacturing a device or deploying a model. It is also about giving users, admins, operators, and customers a reliable way to interact with the product. That is the app layer. With WeWeb, builders can create this layer visually and connect it to the systems behind the product. You can build: MVPs for early validation. Pilot user portals. Customer dashboards. Device management interfaces. Internal production trackers. Quality control tools. AI review workflows. RAG knowledge-base managers. Admin panels. Support consoles. Analytics dashboards. Customer-facing AI apps. WeWeb can support both early prototypes and more production-ready applications. Builders can use WeWeb’s native backend for data, logic, authentication, and workflows, or connect to external systems through APIs, databases, AI services, automation tools, and custom backends. For hardware products, this can mean creating the dashboards and portals around the device. For AI products, it can mean creating the interface, workflow, and monitoring layer around the model. For hybrid hardware + AI products, it can mean connecting device data, AI outputs, user actions, and admin workflows in one application experience. The prototype proves the idea. The production app helps people actually use it. MVP examples built with WeWeb Many builders use WeWeb to move from idea to MVP faster, then keep improving the product once real users are involved. Flexibl launched a financial analytics SaaS MVP in one month using WeWeb, Xano, and Stripe. The product started with six beta testers and converted two into paying customers. Hello Generalist turned a scrappy MVP into a fully functional marketplace in three months with WeWeb and Xano. Aloe Digital built a B2B SaaS MVP for US healthcare professionals from scratch in four weeks, without prior programming experience. Frogcast by Steadysun used WeWeb to build and test an MVP for a solar forecasting product, choosing WeWeb over a Django UI to move faster while keeping technical flexibility. Aby Abraham used WeWeb and Xano to build multiple revenue-generating SaaS products, including one that was acquired and another that reached $150K+ in revenue. Ready to build the app layer for your product? Start building with WeWeb Frequently Asked Questions 1. What is the prototype to production lifecycle? The prototype to production lifecycle encompasses all the stages involved in taking a product from an initial concept or prototype to a fully manufactured and market ready item. It includes research, design, validation, manufacturing setup, and scaling production. 2. Why is Design for Manufacturability (DFM) so important? DFM is crucial because most of a product’s manufacturing cost (around 70 to 80%) is determined during the design phase. By optimizing the design for ease of manufacturing early on, you can significantly reduce costs, improve quality, and shorten your time to market. 3. What is the difference between prototyping and low volume manufacturing? Prototyping is focused on validating a concept and gathering feedback quickly and cheaply with very few units. Low volume manufacturing (or bridge production) is a step after prototyping, where you produce a small batch of products to test your manufacturing processes and supply chain before committing to mass production. 4. How can I reduce risks in my supply chain? Key risk mitigation strategies include dual sourcing critical components from different suppliers or regions, maintaining safety stock of essential parts, and regularly auditing your suppliers. This builds resilience against unexpected disruptions. 5. Why do so many AI models fail to make it into production? Many AI models never get deployed due to a variety of challenges, including a failure to pass real world validation, integration difficulties with existing systems, a lack of scalable infrastructure, and organizational hurdles. Successfully navigating the path from a working model to a production system requires strong MLOps (Machine Learning Operations) practices. 6. How can no code platforms help with the prototype to production process? No code platforms can dramatically speed up the early stages. You can build a functional prototype or MVP in days instead of months, allowing for rapid user testing and validation. For startups and enterprises alike, this means you can test your product market fit and iterate on your idea much faster and with less initial investment. 7. What is the most critical stage in the prototype to production journey? While every stage is important, the early stages of market research and validation are arguably the most critical. Building a product that no one wants is the most common reason for failure. Ensuring strong product market fit before you invest heavily in development and manufacturing is the key to success. 8. What does “Right First Time” quality mean? “Right First Time” is a quality philosophy focused on preventing defects rather than catching them later. It means designing processes and training people to perform tasks correctly on the first attempt, which eliminates costly rework, scrap, and warranty claims. 9. Do hardware products need software before launch? Many do. Hardware products often need dashboards, onboarding flows, device management tools, support consoles, analytics, and customer portals. Even if the core product is physical, the surrounding software can be critical for adoption, support, and post-launch improvement. 10. How can WeWeb help move from prototype to production? WeWeb helps builders create the app layer around a product. That can include MVPs, dashboards, portals, admin panels, AI review tools, internal workflows, and customer-facing applications. Builders can use WeWeb’s native backend or connect to external APIs, databases, AI services, and automation tools. 11. Can I use WeWeb for AI product interfaces? Yes. WeWeb can be used to build AI product interfaces such as prompt tools, review workflows, AI dashboards, knowledge-base managers, customer-facing AI apps, and admin consoles connected to AI APIs or backend workflows.

body_text: KITCHENER, ON , July 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Canadian Solar Inc. title: Docker Log Rotation Configuration Guide | SigNoz
summary: Docker uses the JSON-file logging driver by default. Learn how to configure Docker log rotation with max-size and max-file to control disk usage.
body_text: Docker Log Rotation Configuration Guide | SigNoz Published on: January 15, 2024 Last Updated: July 08, 2026 7 min read It is essential to configure log rotation for Docker containers. Log rotation is not performed by default, and if it’s not configured, logs on the Docker host can build up and eat up disk space. This guide will teach us how to set up Docker log rotation . Logs are an essential piece of telemetry data. Logs can be used to debug performance issues in applications. They produce a thorough list of the events that take place in your application, which can be used to troubleshoot issues and identify the root cause of a problem. With containerization, it is easier to scale applications. But the operation complexity has increased manifolds. Containers are ephemeral. Frequently changing container-based environments are challenging to monitor. Docker logs can help debug performance issues. Applications in Docker containers emit logs through stdout and stderr output streams. The logging driver that you choose can access these streams. Based on your logging driver, you can configure the format and storage of Docker logs. You can also send the emitted logs to a centralized setup using open source log management tools . Before deep-diving into configuring Docker log rotation, let's briefly overview Docker logs. A brief on Docker Logs Logging in Docker is different from applications hosted on physical or virtual hosts. Container environment is dynamic, and troubleshooting is more complex. In Docker, primarily, there are two types of log files. Docker daemon logs These logs are generated by the Docker daemon and located on the host. It provides insights into the state of the Docker platform. Docker container logs Our guide on viewing Docker container logs covers all the logs related to a particular application running in a container. Docker does not impose a size restriction on logging files. Hence they will inevitably increase over time and consume storage if left unchecked. You can imagine the growth of log files over time and the amount of storage they would require in a scenario where you have numerous containers running. Limiting the size and quantity of locally stored log files is the main goal of log rotation. Docker logs must be cycled at predetermined intervals because manually deleting logs is a laborious task. But the first question is, where are Docker logs stored? Where are Docker logs stored? Logs are often kept on the Docker host because containers are stateless (failing to remember or save data from previous actions). Docker uses the JSON-file logging driver by default, and it records all stdout and stderr output in JSON format. Log files are created for each container and are generally stored at: /var/lib/docker/containers/[container-id]/[container-id]-JSON.log Docker provides support for multiple logging drivers. You can check out other logging drivers available. To know your current logging driver for Docker Daemon, run the following command: docker info --format '{{.LoggingDriver}}' Why is Docker Log Rotation needed? Docker log rotation is critical for several reasons: Resource Management: Without log rotation, logs can consume significant disk space, especially in high-traffic environments, leading to system slowdown or failure. As such, it is a good idea for teams to also learn to clear Docker logs manually. Performance Optimization: Regularly rotating logs helps maintain optimal performance of Docker containers and the host system. Security and Compliance: For security-sensitive applications, rotating logs can help manage sensitive data and comply with data retention policies. Simplified Troubleshooting: It makes it easier to analyze recent logs without wading through old, irrelevant data. Configuring Docker Log Rotation Before we get hands-on, do note that rotation is one piece; we have covered other pieces of the puzzle, such as drivers and commands, in our Docker logging overview. Let’s first configure the Docker daemon to a particular log driver. To configure the Docker Daemon to a particular log driver: Step 1: Go to the Docker daemon configuration file location: On Linux: /etc/docker/ directory On Windows: C:\ProgramData\docker\config\daemon.json Step 2: If your logging driver hasn’t been set yet, use the following command to set it up: { "log-driver" : "local" } or { "log-driver" : "json-file" } You can specify any log driver of your choice but Docker recommends using the local logging driver to prevent disk exhaustion because it performs log rotation by default. Step 3: Add configuration for log rotation Add the following code to the daemon.json file after editing or creating it to rotate the log. The final file, when using json-file driver looks like this: { "log-driver" : "json-file" , "log-opts" : { "max-size" : "10m" , "max-file" : "5" } } You can also update the parameters for local logging driver using the same format: { "log-driver" : "local" , "log-opts" : { "max-size" : "10m" , "max-file" : "5" } } Step 4: Save the file and restart docker. systemctl restart docker The change in the default logging driver impacts only the containers created after modifying the daemon configuration. The existing containers carry the initial configuration of the logging driver. In order to update their logging driver for existing containers, they must be recreated with the preferred options. Configuring Log Drivers and Rotation for specific containers To configure a container to use a different logging driver than the Docker daemon’s default, use the --log-driver flag. You need to include the container ID or container name alongside the command. docker run -it --log-driver json-file nginx The --log-driver flag specifies the log driver you are assigning to that container. In the above example, the log driver assigned to the container is the json-file . To find the current logging driver for a running container, if the daemon is using the json-file logging driver, run the following command: docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.LogConfig.Type}}' < CONTAINER > Then to setup log rotation for the specified container, run the below commands: docker run \ --log-driver json-file \ --log-opt max-size = 15m \ --log-opt max-file = 5 \ nginx echo hello world Another way to do this is by running the below command docker run -- log - opt max - size = 15m -- log - opt max - file = 5 nginx : latest Simplifying the above command: docker run -- log - opt max - size = 15m It tells Docker to limit the size of your Docker log file. -- log - opt max - file = 5 It instructs Docker to store no more than 5 log files. When the limit is met, Docker is instructed to destroy the older files. nginx : latest The container image name You can also have a look at the logging options the JSON-file accepts. Final Thoughts In this guide, we learned how to set up Docker log rotation. Container environments are highly dynamic, with multiple layers of abstraction. As a result, it's hard to debug such environments, and logs can play a critical role in providing much-needed visibility into performance issues. Docker provides various terminal commands to interact with Docker logs. You can use your console to view logs while developing your application or debugging a specific scenario. But in production environments, it’s advisable to centralize your logs for storage and analysis. That’s where a log management solution comes into the picture. The first step for efficient log management is log aggregation. Once the logs are aggregated, you need to store them and set them up for analysis. There are multiple log management solutions out there. But which solution is best suited for modern distributed cloud-native applications? SigNoz , a full-stack open-source APM, can help you to store, manage, and analyze logs at scale. It correlates all your telemetry data(logs, metrics, and traces) into a single suite of monitoring. Apart from logs, SigNoz can also help you monitor metrics and traces. Logs management in SigNoz SigNoz is built to support OpenTelemetry natively. OpenTelemetry, an open-source project backed by Cloud Native Computing Foundation , can be used to aggregate and process logs from multiple sources. OpenTelemetry is quietly becoming the world standard for instrumenting cloud-native applications to generate telemetry data. Getting started with SigNoz SigNoz Cloud is the easiest way to run SigNoz. Sign up for a free account and get 30 days of unlimited access to all features. You can also install and self-host SigNoz yourself since it is open-source. With 24,000+ GitHub stars, open-source SigNoz is loved by developers. Find the instructions to self-host SigNoz. Further Reading SigNoz - an open source alternative to DataDog

title: How to Choose the Best Time and Attendance Platform for Multi-Site Construction Companies
summary: Multi-site construction companies size up time and attendance platforms against five criteria: GPS geofencing, offline clock-in, foreman-led crew clock-in, certified payroll support, and multi-site reporting. Asure evaluated Truein, Workyard, WorkMax, SmartBarrel, and Asure Time & Attendance against all five, weighing…
body_text: Multi-site construction companies size up time and attendance platforms against five criteria: GPS geofencing, offline clock-in, foreman-led crew clock-in, certified payroll support, and multi-site reporting. Asure evaluated Truein, Workyard, WorkMax, SmartBarrel, and Asure Time & Attendance against all five, weighing how each platform's data connects to payroll, tax filing, and HR compliance afterward. If you run one job site, watching the gate is enough to know who showed up. If you run three or four active projects at once, with subcontractors rotating through and a foreman splitting time between locations, you cannot verify who is on the clock without a system that does it automatically. Paper timesheets and a foreman's memory do not scale past a handful of workers, and disputes over hours tend to surface at the worst possible time, during payroll week or in the middle of a compliance audit. That is the operational problem every platform in this guide, including Asure Time & Attendance, is built to address. Asure evaluated each platform against those five criteria using only what could be independently confirmed. Where a vendor's feature checked out, it is stated as fact with a source. Where it did not, that gap is flagged rather than guessed at, because a comparison built on assumed checkmarks is worse than no comparison at all. The Five Criteria That Matter for Multi-Site Construction Time Tracking Asure's evaluation framework for multi-site construction time and attendance rests on five criteria, explained one at a time below. GPS geofencing accuracy. GPS geofencing creates a virtual boundary around a job site using GPS coordinates, so a time and attendance app can restrict or verify clock-in and clock-out to only when a worker's device confirms it is inside that boundary. On a tight urban lot, a small fixed radius works fine. On a sprawling highway project or large civil site, a fixed radius that is too small can lock out workers who are legitimately on site. Platforms that let administrators set the radius per site score better here than those with one setting for every job. Offline mode functionality. Offline mode means a worker can clock in or out without cellular or Wi-Fi coverage, with the app storing the event locally and syncing it automatically once connectivity returns. This matters most in rural areas, tunnels, and remote sites where signal is unreliable by nature, not by exception. A platform that requires a live connection at the moment of clock-in will fail exactly when a multi-site operation needs it most. Foreman or crew-lead clock-in workflows. Not every worker on a construction site carries a smartphone, and even those who do may not want to manage individual app logins in the field. A foreman or crew-lead clock-in workflow lets one supervisor clock an entire crew in or out from a single device, which is often the only realistic option for larger crews or workers without company-issued phones. Certified payroll and prevailing wage compliance. Certified payroll is a weekly payroll report required on federally funded construction projects under the Davis-Bacon Act , documenting that workers were paid the applicable prevailing wage for their trade and location, according to the U.S. Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division as of July 2026. Covered contracts over $2,000 require contractors to submit this report, using Form WH-347, weekly, within seven days of the regular pay date for each payroll period, even for weeks when no work was performed. As of July 2026, the federal form is mid-transition: a revised WH-347 became effective in January 2025, and the prior version is stated to remain valid only through September 30, 2026. Any contractor relying on a vendor's certified payroll template should confirm which version is current at dol.gov/agencies/whd/forms/wh347 before publish or bid submission. Not every time and attendance platform generates this report natively, and tracking multiple pay rates across trades and classifications adds a layer that general-purpose time clocks were not built to handle. Multi-site reporting and visibility. Operations managers overseeing several active projects need labor hours, attendance, and overtime visible across every site from a single dashboard, not five separate exports stitched together manually at the end of the week. This criterion is less about any single clock-in event and more about whether the data adds up to something usable once it is collected. Read more about how Asure's construction workforce management platform handles time capture alongside payroll and HR data. Comparing the Platforms at a Glance The table below reflects what could be independently verified as of July 2026. Several feature claims common in secondary blog roundups, including specific checklists for WorkMax and SmartBarrel, could not be confirmed against a primary source for this review. Rather than guess, those cells are marked as unconfirmed. Platform GPS Geofencing Offline Clock-In Foreman or Crew-Lead Clock-In Certified Payroll Support Multi-Site Reporting Asure Time & Attendance Confirmed; GeoPunch mobile capture pairs GPS location with photo verification, with configurable per-site geofencing¹ Confirmed; captures clock-in locally and syncs automatically once connectivity returns¹ Confirmed; crew clocking lets a foreman or supervisor clock an entire crew in or out from a single device¹ Feeds AsureCentral for payroll and tax filing; not certified-payroll-specific Native; connected to payroll and HR data Truein Confirmed; per-site geofence, ~20m minimum radius² Confirmed; GPS and facial recognition capture offline, auto-syncs² Not confirmed* Not confirmed* Not confirmed* Workyard Vendor-reported; GPS tracking tied to job costing Not confirmed* Not confirmed* Partial; payroll exports confirmed, native WH-347 generation unconfirmed Not confirmed* WorkMax Not confirmed* Not confirmed* Not confirmed* Not confirmed* Not confirmed* SmartBarrel Not confirmed* Not confirmed* Not confirmed* Not confirmed* Not confirmed* *Not confirmed means this review could not verify the feature against a primary source as of July 2026. Feature sets change frequently. Confirm current capabilities directly with each vendor before purchasing. ¹ Source: Asure GeoPunch and crew clocking product documentation (help.asureforce.net/display/aft/GeoPunch), July 2026. ² Source: Truein product page (truein.com/geofencing-attendance-system), July 2026. Asure Time & Attendance for Connected Payroll and HR Data Asure Time & Attendance is Asure's timekeeping product, capturing hours through a web clock, mobile punch, badge reader, or biometric clock. It runs as part of AsureCentral, Asure's connected payroll and HR platform, and can also run through AsureWorks, Asure's managed service, for construction companies that would rather have Asure's specialists handle payroll and day-to-day administration. Asure Time & Attendance is included here because it answers a question that matters just as much as any single field feature. Instead of optimizing one clock-in method for site conditions, it treats time capture as one input into a system that also runs payroll, tax filing, and HR compliance. Consider a general contractor running three active job sites with a mix of full-time employees and specialty subcontractors. A foreman approves hours at the end of each week in Asure Time & Attendance. Those approved hours flow into payroll processing on AsureCentral, which handles the multi-jurisdiction tax filing tied to whichever states and localities the sites fall under, and Asure HR Compliance keeps the related documentation current. Nobody exports a spreadsheet and re-keys it into a second system. Strengths: Supports multiple capture methods, web clock, mobile punch, badge reader, biometric clock, and GeoPunch mobile capture, which pairs GPS location with photo verification, letting a company mix methods across office staff, yard workers, and field crews. Confirmed on the field-specific criteria that matter for remote or multi-site work: configurable per-site geofencing through GeoPunch, offline clock-in that stores capture locally and syncs automatically once connectivity returns, and crew clocking that lets a foreman or supervisor clock an entire crew in or out from a single device. Feeds time data directly into payroll processing and tax filing on AsureCentral, removing a manual export step before a payroll run. Pairs with Asure HR Compliance and AsureWorks, so a growing contractor can add managed payroll or HR support later without switching systems. Limitations: Is not marketed as a certified payroll or Davis-Bacon-specific reporting tool. Time data supports payroll and tax processing, but prevailing wage reporting is not its stated specialty. Asure's Verdict: Asure Time & Attendance is the right choice if your core problem is disconnected systems, not just disconnected job sites. If your time data currently lives apart from payroll, tax filing, and HR records, and you want all three in one place, this addresses that gap directly. It also holds up on the field-specific criteria that matter for remote or multi-site crews, GPS-verified mobile capture with photo confirmation, offline clock-in, and crew clocking for foremen managing workers who don't carry individual devices. Best for general contractors and specialty subcontractors that want time tracking connected to payroll and compliance, particularly those who may want AsureWorks to manage payroll administration as the business grows. Pricing is quote-based; contact Asure directly for current rates. Truein for Biometric Verification at Fixed Job Sites Truein is a facial recognition time and attendance app built around verifying identity at a physical point of entry. According to Truein's own product page , its geofencing and offline capture are designed specifically for job-site conditions rather than office use. Strengths: Reduces buddy punching through facial recognition clock-in at fixed entry points such as fabrication yards, warehouses, or permanent site offices. Confirms offline capture: GPS location and facial recognition function without an internet connection and sync automatically once connectivity is restored ( Truein , July 2026). Lets administrators configure a per-site geofence, with a minimum recommended radius of approximately 20 meters for reliable GPS accuracy ( Truein , July 2026). Limitations: Works best in a kiosk or fixed-point verification model where crews pass through a defined access point; open, sprawling sites with multiple entry paths and no fixed checkpoint are a harder fit for your operation. Lacks independently verified information on foreman-batch clock-in, certified payroll reporting, or multi-site dashboard depth as of July 2026. Asure's Verdict: Truein is a strong option if your operation has fixed points of entry, where biometric verification removes any question of who actually clocked in. It is a narrower fit if your crews spread across open terrain with no consistent checkpoint. Pricing is quote-based; contact Truein directly for your specific sites. Workyard for Residential and Light Commercial Projects Workyard is a GPS time tracking and job costing platform marketed to residential and light commercial contractors. According to Workyard's own site, it provides GPS-verified time data with automated payroll exports to platforms including QuickBooks and Gusto. Strengths: Ties GPS-verified time data directly to job costing, useful for contractors tracking labor cost per project rather than just total hours. Reduces manual re-entry into accounting systems through automated payroll export integrations. Limitations: Leaves native certified payroll and WH-347 report generation unconfirmed on Workyard's own product pages as of July 2026. Some secondary sources describe the capability, but none trace to a primary source, so treat it as an open question rather than a settled feature. Lacks independently verified information on offline mode, foreman-batch clock-in, or multi-site reporting depth. Asure's Verdict: Workyard is a reasonable fit if you run residential or light commercial projects and want GPS-verified time data tied to your job costing exports. If certified payroll reporting for a federally funded project is a hard requirement for your bids, get written confirmation of Workyard's current Davis-Bacon capability straight from the vendor rather than relying on this guide or secondary marketing claims. Pricing is quote-based; contact Workyard directly. WorkMax for Equipment-Heavy Operations WorkMax markets itself as a workforce management platform for construction and field-service operations, with modules that extend beyond time tracking into equipment and material tracking. Strengths: Combines labor and equipment tracking, which may suit operations that need to see machine usage alongside crew hours in one place. Limitations: None of the five criteria, GPS geofencing, offline mode, foreman clock-in, certified payroll, or multi-site reporting, could be verified against a primary source as of July 2026. WorkMax's published documentation did not settle these one way or the other for this guide. Asure's Verdict: WorkMax is worth a direct look if tracking equipment usage alongside labor hours is a stated priority for your operation. Ask the vendor to walk through GPS geofencing, offline mode, foreman clock-in, and certified payroll specifically before you commit, since none of the four turned up in a primary source for this guide. Pricing is quote-based; contact WorkMax directly. SmartBarrel for Large-Scale Infrastructure Projects SmartBarrel markets itself as a facial recognition time clock built for large infrastructure and heavy civil construction projects, using physical kiosks positioned at site entry points rather than individual worker devices. Strengths: Captures verified identity at the point of entry through physical kiosks with facial recognition, which can be useful on large sites where many workers and subcontractors move through a limited number of access points. Limitations: Requires equipment at each site under a kiosk-based, hardware-dependent model, a harder fit for smaller projects or highly mobile crews without a fixed entry point. Offline mode, foreman clock-in, certified payroll, and multi-site reporting remain open questions as of July 2026, since none of the four appear in a primary source for this guide. Asure's Verdict: SmartBarrel fits your operation well if you run large infrastructure or heavy civil projects where verifying worker identity at scale, often across many subcontractors, matters more than mobile flexibility. Have the vendor demonstrate the remaining four criteria in person before you sign rather than taking them on faith. Pricing is quote-based; contact SmartBarrel directly. How to Choose the Right Platform for Your Operation If you bid on federally funded projects subject to Davis-Bacon prevailing wage rules, certified payroll reporting is not optional. Verify any platform's current WH-347 support directly against the U.S. Department of Labor's requirements before you sign a contract, not after. If your crews work in areas with unreliable cell coverage, prioritize a platform with confirmed offline clock-in and sync, and get that confirmation in writing rather than assuming it from marketing copy. Asure Time & Attendance and Truein both have verified offline performance as of this review. If your foremen manage crews who do not carry individual smartphones, look for confirmed batch or supervisor-led clock-in, such as Asure Time & Attendance's crew clocking, and have any vendor demonstrate the workflow in action rather than take it on faith. If you need to verify identity at a fixed yard, warehouse, or permanent site office, a kiosk or biometric option, including Asure Time & Attendance's biometric clock, Truein, or SmartBarrel, is built around that use case. If your top priority is getting time and attendance data into the same system that already runs payroll, tax filing, and HR compliance, without a separate export step, that is the specific problem Asure Time & Attendance and AsureCentral solve. If you do not have an in-house payroll team to run that connected system, AsureWorks gives you the option to have Asure's specialists handle payroll and day-to-day administration instead, without putting you into a PEO co-employment structure or handing over control of your workforce decisions. You remain the employer of record either way. See how Asure Time & Attendance connects to payroll and HR Compliance for multi-site construction operations. The Bottom Line For most construction companies running multiple active job sites, the strength that carries the most weight is whether your time and attendance data flows directly into payroll, tax filing, and HR compliance without a separate export step, and that is where Asure Time & Attendance is a legitimate, recommended path, built into AsureCentral, with AsureWorks available if you would rather hand payroll administration to Asure's specialists. Asure Time & Attendance also holds up on the field-specific non-negotiables, not just connected data: GeoPunch mobile capture pairs GPS location with photo verification and configurable per-site geofencing, offline clock-in stores capture locally and syncs automatically once connectivity returns, and crew clocking lets a foreman clock an entire crew in from a single device. Truein has its own verified strengths on two of those same criteria, offline capture and per-site geofencing radius control, confirmed against its own product page as of this review, so it is worth a direct look if your sites are fixed-point and connectivity is inconsistent. Certified payroll support is the one non-negotiable no platform in this guide is built to own outright; confirm current WH-347 support directly against the Department of Labor's requirements before you bid or sign. None of that changes the core case for connected data: start with Asure's time and attendance product page to see how connected time data fits your payroll, tax, and HR compliance needs. Related Questions Can construction workers clock in without a smartphone? Yes. Several platforms support supervisor-led or kiosk-based clock-in that does not require every worker to carry a device. Truein uses facial recognition at fixed kiosks, and SmartBarrel takes a similar hardware-based approach for large sites. Asure Time & Attendance supports web clock, badge reader, biometric clock, and crew clocking, which lets a foreman clock an entire crew in or out from a single device. This matters for construction companies where not every field worker owns or uses a smartphone on the job. What is certified payroll, and which time tracking platforms support it? Certified payroll is a weekly payroll report required on federally funded construction projects under the Davis-Bacon Act, documenting that workers were paid the applicable prevailing wage for their trade and location, per the U.S. Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division as of July 2026. Not every time and attendance platform generates this report natively, and the underlying federal form itself changed in January 2025, with the prior version remaining valid only through September 30, 2026. Asure Time & Attendance is not marketed as a certified-payroll-specific tool, but approved time data feeds AsureCentral for the multi-jurisdiction tax filing work behind a certified payroll report. Confirm current WH-347 support directly with any vendor before you rely on it for a bid. How does GPS geofencing work for construction job sites? GPS geofencing creates a virtual boundary around a job site so a worker can only clock in when their device confirms they are physically inside that perimeter. Most platforms let administrators set the radius per site, which matters on large or irregularly shaped sites where a small fixed radius could exclude workers who are legitimately on site. Truein, for example, recommends a minimum radius of approximately 20 meters for reliable GPS accuracy. Asure Time & Attendance supports configurable per-site geofencing through its GeoPunch mobile capture, which pairs GPS location with photo verification; confirm the specific radius settings available for your sites directly with Asure. What happens if a construction worker clocks in where there is no cell service? Platforms with true offline mode store the clock-in event locally on the device and sync it automatically once connectivity returns. Truein has confirmed offline capture through GPS and facial recognition that syncs on reconnect, and Asure Time & Attendance offers its own confirmed offline clock-in with the same local-capture-and-sync approach, both useful for tunnels, remote sites, and rural areas with inconsistent coverage. Construction companies weighing offline capability should also consider whether that time data needs to connect directly to payroll and tax filing without manual re-entry, which is the specific problem Asure Time & Attendance is built to solve.
