title: Before You Expand, Read the Market
summary: Price transparency data is changing how health systems evaluate growth opportunities. Learn how reimbursement intelligence can inform market expansion, service line planning, and investment decisions.
body_text: What the Market Is Already Telling You About Where to Grow For most health system executives, growth decisions have always carried some degree of uncertainty. Determining whether to enter a new market, launch a service line, or invest in a new setting of care required assembling fragmented estimates, relying on consultants, and making assumptions that were difficult to validate before significant capital was committed. That dynamic has shifted. Price transparency mandates now require payers to publish negotiated commercial reimbursement rates through machine-readable files (MRFs). For health system strategy and business development teams, this is a meaningful change in a positive direction. The market intelligence that once required months of engagement to assemble is now, with the right tools, available in days. The question is whether health systems are using it. Growth Decisions Deserve Better Inputs The traditional approach to evaluating a new market or service line looks something like this: survey comparable markets, model revenue based on internal assumptions, consult with advisors, and hope the underlying data is close enough. The problem is not the process itself. The problem is that the inputs have historically been too thin, too slow, and too disconnected from what the market is actually paying. Price transparency data changes that calculus. When MRF data is properly cleaned, normalized, and enriched, health systems can answer questions that previously had no reliable answer: What are commercial payers reimbursing for a specific service in a target market? How does the reimbursement landscape compare across multiple markets under consideration? Where do competing providers sit relative to Medicare benchmarks in that geography? What is the payer concentration in the market, and how does that affect negotiating position? These answers represent much more than marginal refinements to the planning process. They are the critical foundational inputs that reduce guesswork and sharpen the business case—all before capital decisions are made. A Smarter Framework for Market Evaluation Consider a health system evaluating three potential markets for a new ambulatory surgery center. Historically, the comparison would rely on demographic data, utilization estimates, and anecdotal intelligence from market participants. Today, the same analysis can be grounded in actual reimbursement data. Across four dimensions, price transparency data can help quantify the relative attractiveness of each market: The reimbursement level attainable for the new care setting The degree of market saturation among existing competitors A site-of-care cost differential that gives payers a financial incentive to redirect volume to a lower cost The payer concentration that will shape negotiating leverage once the system is operational. This kind of structured comparison does not replace judgment but it does replace guesswork with evidence, which is a significant upgrade for any growth decision. Service Line Planning Benefits Too The same logic applies when evaluating whether to add a new clinical service. Before negotiating rates with payers to support a new offering, strategy teams can use MRF data to map the current reimbursement landscape for the relevant procedure codes. Understanding where the market pays, at what percentile comparable providers are positioned, and how wide the spread is between top and bottom performers gives the contracting team a far stronger foundation heading into those conversations. The result is a more defensible business case, a more credible negotiating position, and a clearer picture of realistic revenue expectations, all before a single dollar of capital has been deployed. The Competitive Advantage Is in the Application The reality is the price transparency data does not create a strategic advantage simply by existing. The advantage accrues to health systems that invest in the infrastructure and expertise to make that data usable—and actually use it. Turning raw MRF files into reliable market intelligence requires ingestion at scale, normalization across code sets, claims-driven filtering to eliminate phantom rates, and enrichment with provider and geographic context. Health systems that build or partner for this capability are gaining something their competitors may not yet have: the ability to evaluate opportunities with precision, move faster on the right ones, and avoid costly commitments in markets where the economics do not support them. The inputs are now available. The competitive advantage comes from knowing how to use them. Ready to see what the market is telling you about your next growth opportunity? title: $58M recuperados: el impacto de reintentos inteligentes sobre la mora en seguros
summary: Una aseguradora con 10.000 pólizas podría estar dejando $58M CLP sobre la mesa cada año. No porque los asegurados no quieran pagar, sino porque nadie los contac
body_text: Cuando un cobro rebota, la mayoría de las aseguradoras tardan a verificarlo por su solución de pagos. No hay un reintento automático, no se comunica a tiempo con el asegurado, y la prima no se cobra. Pero no es solo ese mes. El mismo asegurado puede volver a fallar el siguiente, por la misma tarjeta vencida, la misma cuenta sin fondos o los mismos datos desactualizados. Si esto se repite a escala, con miles de pólizas y decenas de cobros rebotados, el problema pasa a ser estructural. ¿Cuánto cuesta esto? Una cartera de 10.000 pólizas con una prima mensual de $60.000 pesos factura $600M al mes. Si el 8% de esos cobros falla y no se recupera, la fuga mensual es de $48M. Recuperar solo un 10% adicional de ese monto equivale a $4.8M mensuales, es decir aproximadamente $58M anuales. Ese es el impacto de cobrar mejor. No depende de vender más pólizas ni subir precios, sino de de recuperar plata que la cartera ya generó y que el proceso actual está dejando ir. ¿Y cuando el proceso funciona en tiempo real? Con Recurring Payments de Fintoc, cada rechazo de cobro se detecta en tiempo real, activando reintentos automáticos de forma inmediata o, de ser necesario, el envío de un link de pago al asegurado. Sin esperar reportes batch del día siguiente, la gestión de cobranza comienza en el momento en que ocurre el rechazo. En la práctica, eso se traduce en cuatro cosas concretas: Prima + suscripción en un solo flujo : el asegurado contrata, paga la primera prima y deja enrolado su medio de pago sin pasos separados. Reintentos inteligentes : cuando el cobro falla, el sistema evalúa el tipo de rechazo y reintenta cuando tiene más probabilidad de salir. Mensajería automática : el asegurado recibe un aviso con link de pago para regularizar, sin que el equipo tenga que llamar a nadie. Visibilidad en tiempo real : el estado de cada cobro en el dashboard y vía API, sin esperar el reporte del día. La mora deja de ser un costo que se asume y pasa a ser un número que se gestiona. ¿Cuánto estás dejando sin recuperar? Los $58M CLP son un ejemplo. title: How to build a credit ledger that scales
summary: Metering token usage needs a different type of infrastructure. This article is about how to build a counter and ledger that works at high throughput and concurrency.
body_text: Introduction When we think about charging for AI applications and agents, we default to "usage-based billing". And while it's clear that tokens should be monetized this way, the infrastructure people are actually building to support this looks completely different from the existing systems that phrase was coined for. Existing billing services assumed that billing was asynchronous. You send events that are tallied up and added to the end of a monthly invoice. This worked well for compute and infrastructure. The most common form of AI billing, however, is "quota-based": a form of usage-billing where synchronous access decision needs to be made in every request path before tokens are spent. This is the business model behind growing companies like Cursor, Lovable and OpenAI (you can even read about Codex's billing architecture in this blog by Jonah Cohen). Customers buy some amount of usage upfront (usually in the form of credits), use them up, then hit a hard limit . These limits are a piece of state in constant flux: plan changes, billing cycles, user controls, promotional grants and other business logic. What do you need? The infrastructure behind our billing has to satisfy three conditions at once: low-latency access decisions on whether a customer can do something (ie, use a credit), a provably correct and auditable record of their usage, and with all of it working under high throughput (millions to billions of monthly events) and concurrency. This article is aimed at AI companies on their second or third rewrite of billing. We will cover: Understanding the counter and ledger, and why you need both Using a cache to keep access decisions fast Tracking usage under load, and why synchronous deduction is needed Handling resets, expiry, and usage analytics Since credits are the most common way of billing for AI tokens, we'll use this as the example going forward. However, the principles apply to any model where quotas are enforced. Real-time access decisions A reasonable first approach would be to ask: can't we just aggregate over all a user's usage events to see if someone has remaining credits when checking a request? This doesn't work for real-time enforcement (we've seen it tried!). Different plans have different limits, rollover logic, expirations. The query becomes complex, slow, and very hard to debug or iterate on. The solution is the counter: typically a static value for the remaining balance of credits or usage, and when that's positive (with some nuance for cases like overages) the action is allowed. The counter The first thing to consider is your data model for credits and balances. Imagine you have a plan which offers 100 credits every month. You would probably start with a schema that looks like this: user_id plan balance cus_001 pro 847 cus_002 free 12 cus_003 scale 4,203 cus_004 pro 560 Now what happens if you want to add single-purchase top ups? You might think to add another column topup_balance to your table. This works for exactly one new credit type. The moment a bucket needs rules of its own; top-ups that expire after 6 months, promotional credits, 3-month rollovers, a daily refresh, a single number stops being enough. Each bucket has its own balance, deduction rules, reset cycles and expiration dates. Therefore, a better approach is to treat each bucket of credits as a separate row within the table: each with its own source, balance, period and expiration date. When determining a user's counter balance, you aggregate over these rows. user_id source balance resets_at expires_at usr_1a2b subscription 100 2026-07-01 null usr_3c4d subscription 100 2026-07-01 null usr_3c4d top_up 250 null 2027-06-05 usr_5e6f subscription 100 2026-07-01 null The obvious place to keep this is your primary database. Balances and plan config already live in Postgres, so you query it directly: sum the customer's credit grant rows, compare against the cost, apply any plan rules, return allow or deny. This is correct and simple, and for many products it's all you ever need. The cost is latency. Every request runs a full aggregation, which is fine at low volume but costly when the check gates every AI call. Introducing a cache The fix is to split the read path from the source of truth. Keep authoritative balances in Postgres, but serve the access check from an in-memory store like Redis. You can maintain a single derived value per customer, their spendable balance, so the check is one key lookup rather than a query with joins. That value is seeded from Postgres. On a cache miss (a new customer, an evicted key, a cold start) you run the full aggregation over their grant rows once, write the result to Redis, and serve every subsequent check from memory. Plan rules that gate the decision, like whether overage is allowed, can be cached alongside the balance so the whole allow/deny resolves without touching the database. Reads stay sub-20ms even at high throughput, and the hot path no longer contends with writes to your primary DB. The trade off is that speed comes at a cost: Redis is now a cache that can drift from the truth in Postgres. Recording usage The counter told us the user can proceed so now we need to record what the user actually did. For that, we add a ledger. The ledger is the durable, record of what happened at each event, and why. It's the source of truth for usage: the thing you replay and reconcile against, and what makes the system provably correct. The core operation is a single deduction, and it has to be atomic. In one database transaction, you decrement the counter balance and insert the ledger row. They commit together or not at all, so you never end up with a balance change that isn't accounted for, or a record with no matching deduction. A single deduction may span several balance rows, all committed in that same transaction. Deducting from a balance (or many balances together) When you first build a credit system, decrementing a counter starts by updating a single row. However, now that we have multiple credit balances (monthly credits + one off credits), there's waterfall logic required when deducting. For example, you might want to: Expiration : deduct from monthly credits first, then any one-off top-ups Pooled balances : Spend a seat-level balance first, then draw from an org-level pool Overage logic : Use up granted free credits first, then dip into billable overages const deductCredits = async ({ userId , amount }) => { const { monthly , oneoff } = await getBalances (userId); const fromMonthly = Math. min (monthly, amount); const fromOneOff = amount - fromMonthly; await db. query ( ` UPDATE credits SET monthly_balance = monthly_balance - ${ fromMonthly }, oneoff_balance = oneoff_balance - ${ fromOneOff } WHERE user_id = ${ userId } ` ); }; To make this atomic, you must lock the rows on read using SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. This blocks concurrent requests on the same user, forcing them to queue up and execute serially. However, that per-account locking is exactly what makes the simple, synchronous version hard to scale. The lock plus the hot-path DB write mean that under load, requests for the same user pile up, and the database becomes the bottleneck. How you fix that depends on one question: can you tolerate the balance lagging reality for a short window? Asynchronous deduction with a queue If a brief lag between spending and the balance updating is acceptable, you can take the deduction off the hot path. The counter approves, you emit an event carrying a stable idempotency key, and you return to the user immediately. A background worker consumes those events and runs the atomic decrement-plus-ledger-insert transaction afterwards. The queue (Kafka, SQS, a Redis stream) absorbs bursts so writes reach Postgres at a rate it can handle, and partitioning by account serializes each user's debits so concurrent requests still can't race to spend the same credits. The idempotency key is what makes this safe to retry: if a worker crashes or an event is redelivered, the key lets the transaction no-op on anything already applied. Once it commits, refresh the Redis counter so the fast read reflects the new balance. Why synchronous deduction is needed AI workloads and agents can be long-running, expensive and spun up concurrently. This makes asynchronous deduction a problem. To illustrate, imagine 5 sub-agents running in parallel: A user has 600 credits remaining Each of the 5 agent runs costs 500 credits All 5 requests read the counter before the deductions settle, so all 5 are approved This allows the user to dramatically overspend their balance because the counter had a delayed update. In these cases, the flow you need looks more like this: Request is made to spin up a sub-agent Estimate the cost (eg 500 credits) and immediately deduct it from the user's balance up front Process the request Adjust the actual usage if it succeeds, refund the deduction if it fails We call this lock-and-release at Autumn, but it's really just a synchronous deduction flow. enqueue ledger batch job · async 4 reqs ×500 Redis atomic counter 600 100 Lua: decrement + enqueue ClickHouse ledger append-only insert atomic with deduct Postgres batch sync source of truth eventually consistent ✗ rejected ×3 insufficient balance When we tried to build this on Postgres directly, transactions sharply limited throughput. Running even a couple of hundred deductions per second wasn't feasible. And once you add additional balances like rollovers, you span multiple tables and need joins, which limits concurrency further. To solve this, we added the ability to deduct from our counters in Redis using Lua scripts. All credit reads and writes happen on Redis, and each write is added to a batch job that syncs balances back to Postgres. Inside the Lua script, we enqueue a ledger insertion event. Writes stay atomic and extremely fast, typically sub-20ms, even at high throughput. But as with any infra decision, there are always trade-offs: Atomic with the ledger event, but not durable. The Lua script commits the decrement and the enqueued ledger insert together, so there's never a balance change without a matching event, but that's an in-memory guarantee. There is a drift-risk on a Redis failure. Keeping Redis and Postgres consistent is its own project. We kept Redis as a read/write cache rather than the source of truth, and there's real complexity in reconciling the two, with plenty of race conditions to handle. Redis isn't a silver bullet. Choosing the right data type, watching costs, and deciding normalized vs de-normalized storage all matter. It's single-threaded, so one slow operation can bottleneck the whole system, and because writes are serial, any atomic system has a throughput ceiling, a single hot user can saturate it. Resets and expiry In addition to a static value, every balance row can have a reset cycle and an expiry. A reset is a recurring grant refreshing: the balance returns to its granted allowance at the start of each cycle. An expiry is credits disappearing permanently. A rollover is just the two composed: leftover balance at a reset converts into a new bucket with its own expiry, rather than vanishing. There are a few ways to design this: Stripe webhooks The simplest way to handle credit resets and expiry would be to listen to Stripe's webhooks, such as invoice.paid or invoice.created . This approach is great because it ties credits directly to when the subscription renews, which minimizes drift. However, it offers limited customizability. For instance, it won't work if your users are on an annual subscription but have their credits reset monthly, or you grant credits on a different cycle (eg, 5 hour rate limits). Cron job You can also spin up a cron job that queries the DB for users that are due for a reset (in the above case, it's a simple next_reset_at < NOW() ). Depending on how granular you want resets to be, you can either run this minutely, hourly or daily. Apart from adding another service, the other concern is that query time will grow linearly with your user base. At some point, you will need to optimize it. Lazy resets The final way you can handle resets is through a lazy strategy. Every time you fetch your user's credits, you do an in-memory check of whether they are due for a reset, and if so then perform the DB update. Lazy resets tend to age the best and work well in most cases, but the downside is that you don't have an accurate trigger for when credits are reset, and so aren't able to perform actions like sending out notifications to users when their credits refresh. In practise, you'll likely end up using multiple of these techniques. At Autumn, for posting overage bills to Stripe invoices, we have to rely on their webhooks. For sending events and emails ( balance.reset ), we'll use a cron. For most standard balance resets, we'll use the lazy approach. We have guards in place to make sure resets stay aligned with the billing cycle. Analytics and Reporting Postgres is the right home for balances and the deduction ledger, where you need transactional guarantees, but it's a bad fit for analytical questions: usage over time, per-feature breakdowns, reconciliation across millions of events. This is a different kind of aggregation from the counter's: the counter resolves a single customer's current spendable balance on the hot path, whereas these run offline over historical events. For that, the events can be sent to a columnar store like ClickHouse. The cleanest way to keep the two in step is to treat ClickHouse as another consumer of the event stream you're already emitting, rather than dual-writing from your application: each deduction (or raw usage event) lands on the stream, the processor commits it to Postgres, and ClickHouse ingests from that same stream independently. ClickHouse is only powerful if you put the time in, though. You can't just create a table, start ingesting events, and call it a day. A few things we've had to work through: Pre-aggregating common queries with materialized views. For instance, hourly or daily credit usage. Being careful about properties on usage events. Low-cardinality fields (like AI model) are straightforward, but unbounded fields like request IDs get expensive quickly. Planning around backfills and corrections. Updating historical events in ClickHouse is possible, but we've spent days on jobs that felt like they should've taken an hour. Conclusion Despite how complex a billing system can get at scale, none of this has to be built at once. The right move is to build for the stage you're at, and most products can start with everything in a single DB. What stays constant though is the shape: a fast counter to decide access, and a durable ledger that makes usage provably correct. By getting this right early, later optimizations can be slotted in when needed. A good billing experience won't make users love your product, but a bad one can make them hate it. Ultimately, it's one part of your app that just has to be correct, so before letting your coding agents run wild, it's worth spending a little time on the system design. Another important aspect is your pricing and billing data model, and how you can ship changes to pricing without a rebuild. You can read more about that in our post on how to make a flexible billing system .

title: Improved performance and model support with GGUF
summary: Ollama 0.30 is now available with improved performance and GGUF model compatibility through llama.cpp. This augments Ollama's MLX engine on Apple silicon, bringing support to more models on a wider range of hardware.
body_text: Ollama 0.30 is now available with improved performance and GGUF model compatibility through llama.cpp . This augments Ollama’s MLX engine on Apple silicon, bringing support to more models on a wider range of hardware. Performance across more GPUs Faster throughput on NVIDIA hardware With Ollama 0.30 , performance on NVIDIA hardware is now up to 20% faster, leveraging optimizations contributed by the NVIDIA and llama.cpp teams. Tested with the Gemma 4 26B model running on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 using the Q4_K_M quantization. Wider hardware support with Vulkan Vulkan is now enabled by default, extending Ollama’s GPU acceleration to a wider range of hardware, including AMD and Intel devices. More users can now run models on the GPU out of the box, without installing vendor-specific libraries. Support for more models Ollama 0.30 expands compatibility with the GGUF ecosystem, so more models run out of the box—including model families such as LFM and Prism , as well as fine-tuned models published by Unsloth . Run GGUF models from Hugging Face To use a model, first download the GGUF file or a directory containing GGUF files. Next, create a Modelfile with the FROM command pointing to the path of the GGUF file (or directory): FROM ./my-model.Q4_K_M.gguf Then create and run the model: ollama create -f Modelfile my-model ollama run my-model Coding agents and assistants If a model supports tool calling, that capability carries over to Ollama. You can use these models with your favorite coding agents and personal assistants in a single command. Claude Code ollama launch claude --model my-model Hermes Agent ollama launch hermes --model my-model OpenClaw ollama launch openclaw --model my-model To verify that a GGUF file supports tool calling, look for the tools capability with ollama show : ollama show my-model Acknowledgements We’d like to acknowledge the work done by Georgi Gerganov and the llama.cpp maintainer teams, as well as hardware partners including NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, and Intel, who have worked hard to optimize performance with the GGML ecosystem on their respective platforms. If you have any feedback, join Ollama’s Discord or reach out at hello@ollama.com.

title: Prediction Markets: How They Work and What US Investors Should Know
summary: How do prediction markets work? Learn how event contracts turn real-world outcomes into tradable probabilities and compare leading platforms for US traders.
body_text: A prediction market lets participants trade contracts tied to the outcome of real-world events, from elections to interest-rate decisions. Prices move as new information arrives, turning collective forecasts into a live, tradable probability. If you're wondering how do prediction markets work and where they fit next to stocks and options, this guide covers the mechanics, the leading platforms, and the safeguards US traders should understand, in a clear, no-hype format. Table of Contents Part 1: How Do Prediction Markets Work? Part 2: How Are Prediction Markets Different from Gambling? Part 3: Popular Prediction Market Platforms for US Traders FAQs The Bottom Line Part 1: How Do Prediction Markets Work? Definition: A prediction market is an exchange-traded marketplace where participants buy and sell contracts whose value is tied to the outcome of a specific future event. Each contract typically settles at $1 if the event happens and $0 if it doesn't, so the current price reads directly as the market-implied probability. Prediction markets convert opinions into prices. When you buy a "Yes" contract at $0.62, the market is effectively saying there's a 62% chance the event occurs. As traders react to news, polls, and data, that price updates in real time — which is exactly what makes a prediction market such a fast, transparent forecasting tool. The Core Mechanics: Contracts, Shares, and Settlement Most US prediction markets use binary event contracts (also called yes/no shares or event contracts). Here's the structure: Contract: A claim on a clearly defined outcome (e.g., "Will the Fed cut rates in September?"). Price range: $0.00 to $1.00 per share, mirroring 0% to 100% probability. Settlement: At expiration, winning shares pay $1.00; losing shares pay $0.00. Order book: Buyers and sellers are matched by an exchange, with liquidity often supported by market makers. Your profit is the difference between your entry price and the settlement value, minus fees. Buy "Yes" at $0.40, and if the event resolves true, each share pays $1.00 — a $0.60 gain per share. A Step-by-Step Prediction Markets Investment Guide Here's how do prediction markets work in a single trade, start to finish: Pick an event. You find a contract: "Will nonfarm payrolls beat forecasts this month?" Read the price. "Yes" trades at $0.55, implying a 55% market probability. Place your order. You buy 100 "Yes" shares for $55 total (plus any fees). Wait for resolution. The data releases and beats expectations, so the contract resolves "Yes." Collect settlement. Your 100 shares pay $100. Gross profit: $45 before fees. If the data had missed, the shares would settle at $0 and you'd lose the $55 stake. That capped, defined-risk structure is central to how these contracts behave. Why Prices Reflect Real Probabilities Prediction markets are often praised for the "wisdom of crowds." Because traders put real capital behind their views, the market aggregates dispersed information — polls, expert models, insider sentiment, and breaking news — into one number. Academic research and event-forecasting studies have repeatedly shown that well-designed prediction market prices can rival or beat individual expert forecasts. That forecasting accuracy is why hedgers, analysts, and everyday traders watch these markets closely. Part 2: How Are Prediction Markets Different From Gambling? Quick answer: Prediction markets differ from gambling because they are exchange-traded, regulated financial instruments used for forecasting and hedging, where prices reflect real probabilities and you trade against other participants. Gambling is a fixed-odds wager set by a house, structured for entertainment, with odds built to favor the operator. Prediction Markets vs. Gambling: Side-by-Side Feature Prediction Market Traditional Gambling Structure Exchange-traded event contracts House-set fixed odds Pricing Set by supply and demand (live probability) Set by the operator with built-in margin Counterparty Other traders on the exchange The house/casino/sportsbook Primary purpose Forecasting, hedging, information Entertainment Regulation (US) CFTC-regulated exchanges for many contracts State gaming commissions Exit before outcome Yes — sell your position anytime Usually no — bet is locked Risk profile Defined risk, capped at stake Defined risk, capped at stake Regulation and Oversight In the United States, legitimate prediction market platforms operate as CFTC-regulated designated contract markets (DCMs) , the same regulatory category used for other derivatives exchanges. This oversight covers contract listing, settlement rules, and market conduct. When you use a prediction market through a US brokerage, your securities activity and cash may also fall under separate protections like SIPC membership and FINRA regulation — a layer traditional sports betting simply doesn't offer. Part 3: Popular Prediction Market Platforms for US Traders Choosing a prediction market platform comes down to regulation, fees, contract selection, and how well event trading integrates with the rest of your portfolio. Below is our ranked breakdown for US traders. 1. Webull — Prediction Market Platform for US Investors Webull stands out because it pairs event trading with a full-featured, regulated brokerage — so your prediction market activity lives alongside stocks, ETFs, and options in one account, on one platform. For traders who want forecasting exposure and a serious investing toolkit, that integration is the differentiator. Platform Overview Webull is a US brokerage built for active, self-directed traders. Securities are offered through Webull Financial LLC, a member of SIPC and FINRA, which means eligible securities accounts carry standard SIPC protection and the firm operates under FINRA oversight. The platform is known for commission-free equities trading, advanced charting, and a mobile-first experience that scales up to desktop. Why Choose Webull for Prediction Markets One unified account: Trade seamlessly between stocks, options, futures, and prediction markets — no separate apps or wallets to fund. Around-the-clock event trading: Markets stay open across sports, finance, and global events, so you can trade as breaking information hits rather than waiting for a fixed close. Exit early, settle instantly: Don't wait for the final whistle. Lock in gains or limit losses by closing your position before the market resolves, with settlement the moment you exit. Programmatic trading via OpenAPI: Deploy algorithmic strategies, automate sentiment analysis, and execute event contracts programmatically using the Webull OpenAPI . Regulated, transparent infrastructure: Backed by a FINRA member broker-dealer with SIPC membership on the securities side. Built for volatility: Every play on the field and every breaking headline shifts the market in real time — position yourself ahead of the curve. How to Get Started in Three Steps Open your Events Account. Sign up on Webull in a few minutes to unlock prediction markets. Already a Webull user? Activate your Events account directly from your profile. Choose your position. Select an event or matchup you're following, pick a "Yes" or "No" contract based on your view, and trade your stance anytime before the market closes. Payout or exit early. Cash out before expiration to secure gains, or hold until the market settles. If your position finishes in your favor, funds are credited directly to your account. 2. Kalshi — Dedicated CFTC-Regulated Event Exchange Kalshi is a US, CFTC-regulated exchange focused purely on event contracts across economics, weather, and current events. It's a strong specialist choice, though it lacks the integrated stock and options environment a full brokerage provides. 3. Polymarket — High-Volume, Broad Event Coverage Polymarket is known for wide event coverage and deep liquidity on popular markets. US traders should carefully confirm current availability and regulatory status before participating. 4. PredictIt — Long-Running Political Markets PredictIt has historically focused on political and election contracts under a specific regulatory arrangement, with position caps that limit larger traders. Platform Comparison Table Platform Best For Integrated Stocks/Options US Regulatory Framing Webull All-in-one trading + events Yes SIPC member, FINRA-regulated broker-dealer Kalshi Pure event trading No CFTC-regulated exchange Polymarket Broad event variety No Confirm current US status PredictIt Political markets No Specialized arrangement FAQs 1. What is a prediction market in simple terms? A prediction market is a marketplace where you trade contracts on the outcome of future events. Each contract's price, between $0 and $1, reflects the market's estimated probability of that event happening. 2. Are prediction markets legal in the US? Many prediction market contracts trade legally on CFTC-regulated exchanges in the US. Legality depends on the platform, the contract type, and current regulation, so always confirm a platform's status before trading. 3. How do prediction markets work for beginners? You pick an event, buy "Yes" or "No" shares at their current price, and hold until the event resolves. Winning shares pay $1.00 each; losing shares pay $0.00. You can often sell before resolution. 4. Can you make money on prediction markets? Yes, it's possible to profit if your forecasts are accurate and you manage fees and risk, but losses are equally possible. Contracts can settle at $0, so only risk capital you can afford to lose. The Bottom Line Prediction markets turn real-world events into transparent, tradable probabilities, and they're distinct from gambling in structure, purpose, and regulation. If you want event trading integrated with a full, regulated brokerage, Webull brings it together with stocks, options, advanced tools, and SIPC-member protection. title: Creating, testing and releasing your first iOS subscription product and app to the App Store
summary: From App Store Connect, to TestFlight and everything in-between, follow this all-in-one guide to get your next idea into production
body_text: Launching an app and earning that initial revenue represents an exciting milestone. However, the path to release can feel overwhelming. This comprehensive guide walks through each essential step, from initial setup through App Store publication. The process covers: Creating an Apple developer account Setting up a new app in App Store Connect Configuring subscription products in App Store Connect Displaying products using Superwall Testing through TestFlight Preparing for App Store review Publishing to the App Store Prerequisites This guide assumes familiarity with Xcode and the ability to build and run apps in the iOS simulator. You should have an app under development ready to monetize. Note that this is not a programming guide but rather focuses on making your existing app testable with real products and deployment-ready. Create a developer account with Apple If you lack an active developer account, visit Apple's enrollment page and complete registration before proceeding. title: 7 best image editing APIs compared by workflow
summary: Compare the 7 best image editing APIs by workflow, scale, and use case. Find the right API for e‑commerce, app integrations, or production automation.
body_text: The best image editing API for your business depends entirely on your existing workflow: how often you edit images, how many images you edit at once, which edits you make, and where images need to be placed at the end of the editing process. There is no one best image editing API—the right tool for you fits into your workflow to create higher quality images faster and at scale. For that reason, this image editing API comparison focuses on workflows, not features. We compare tools based on their consistency, scalability, and integration into existing tools and processes. Other API benefits—like artistic creativity, prompt engineering capabilities, or novelty uses—are useful for single edits, but don’t affect an image editing API’s ability to build end-to-end visual production pipelines. So what are the best image editing APIs by workflow? We compared 7 tools with 7 distinct workflow fits. Tool Best use case API model Pricing Photoroom Developing end-to-end production workflows for e‑commerce Workflow-oriented Basic plans start at $20/month for $1,000 credits PicsArt Automating creative campaign imagery with text and templates Creative editing Plans start at $5 for 1,000 credits (monthly subscription) Gemini Analyzing images for brand and marketplace compliance Multi-modal AI Free plans available Remove.bg Removing and replacing backgrounds for marketplace catalogs Single-purpose Basic, pay-as-you-go plans start at $1/credit Jasper Editing and improving product imagery Workflow-oriented Plans start at $59/month Claid Standardizing and optimizing large batches of imagery Workflow-oriented Up to 50 credits free Paid plans start at $59/1,000 credits Open AI Generating various lifestyle and campaign images from a single photo Multi-modal AI Plans start at $5.00/1M input tokens What is an image editing API? Image editing APIs allow developers and teams to integrate image editing capabilities into external software applications. The benefit doesn’t lie solely in the integration; an image editing API also enables teams to automate and unify workflows. This is the core differentiator between the best image editor APIs. Single-purpose image APIs allow you to scale one editing function, like background removal, over thousands of images. Creative editing APIs automate the enhancement or editing of images for lifestyle photography or campaign imagery. Multi-modal AI APIs can interpret a variety of inputs, from video to text and images, to create custom workflows. And workflow-oriented visual APIs focus on automating and scaling product photography workflows from start to finish, from RAW file to CMS. This is an important distinction to make when choosing the best image editing API for your business—and not just because incomplete or intensive workflows are frustrating. Most APIs are priced per output, which means the wrong tool will cost you time and money. This is why Photoroom is a top choice for e‑commerce sellers: their API automates their entire product photography workflow in a single call. To see how it can speed up your production workflows, try Photoroom's API today. How we evaluated the best image editing APIs We examined each API’s abilities across these core factors, with a strong emphasis on scalability and workflow fit. The top image editing APIs meet most or all of these criteria. Output consistency Does the image editing API reliably create consistent results across edits? Is it able to apply workflows consistently, no matter the image subject? Inconsistent results create workflow gaps that image editing APIs should address. Workflow integration Does the tool offer features that integrate into key editing processes? We looked for tools that allow teams to resize, expand, and reuse images across marketplaces and platforms—a core part of visual production workflows. Scalability Does the image editing API reduce time spent on edits by providing features that support scale? Many of the tools below offer batch editing and automatic workflows. Suitability for real products Is this image editing API suitable for production environments where images directly impact revenue, brand consistency, and customer experience? Industries like e‑commerce, apps, and SaaS rely heavily on workflows that reliably deliver production-ready outputs. Automation might as well be manual when you have to fine-tune every image. Developer experience Most image editing APIs can generate visually stunning images, especially with AI. But an API experience that works predictably is more impactful than an image editing API that delivers occasional “magic” results without control. We looked for tools created by trusted, experienced developers. The best image editing APIs compared The best image editing APIs are unique in their use cases; while many of them offer similar features, the details that differentiate them are essential to understanding which one is right for you. Each image editing API in this list fits a different production model. Photoroom, Jasper, and Claid’s APIs are suitable for workflow production, Gemini and OpenAI are multimodal AI APIs, PicsArt is a creative image editing API, and Remove.bg is a single-purpose image API. Let’s take a look at what that means for your workflows. 1. Photoroom What it does best: Photoroom’s workflow-oriented API supports end-to-end visual production pipelines. With multiple AI models and flexible workflows, Photoroom helps teams process large image volumes, standardize catalogs, enforce visual guidelines, ensure marketplace compliance, and deliver high-quality product photography at scale. E‑commerce teams experimenting with APIs can experience Photoroom’s first hand through the Marketplace API Playground . Ideal use case: You manage an online retailer’s product catalog across multiple platforms and marketplaces. Integrate Photoroom’s API into your existing content management tools, and create an automatic workflow to remove backgrounds, reposition subjects, refine images, apply your brand kit, and ensure marketplace compliance across thousands of images at once. Pros: Reuse images across platforms and use cases with automatic aspect-ratio scaling and formatting. Combine various API solutions ( Remove Background API , Image Editing API, and Generate Background API, among others) to create powerful custom and automatic workflows with a single endpoint. Upload images from local directories, Google Drive and Google Sheets, Excel spreadsheets, Zapier, Make.com, and iOS and macOS Shortcuts. Process images at exceptional speed with a median latency of 350ms and support 60 images per minute. Integrate Photoroom’s API directly into existing DAMs, PIMs, CMSs, and e‑commerce platforms to maintain uninterrupted visual production workflows. PicsArt What it does best: The PicsArt API offers a suite of AI-powered editing tools that integrate with your existing apps and workflows. With integrations with Instagram, WordPress, and other content apps, PicsArt adds editing support to workflows that drive creative imagery. Ideal use case: You manage social media marketplaces for a large cosmetics company. You need to reuse lifestyle imagery from your photography team to create custom graphics for social media listings. Use one of PicsArt API’s workflow templates to automatically detect new images in OneDrive, remove their backgrounds, apply branded templates and promotional overlays, and export resized versions for Instagram, TikTok, and Meta ads. Pros: PicsArt’s API integrates with Google Sheets, WordPress, Instagram, ChatGPT, and other tools your business already uses. Delivers consistent, scalable outputs across images, tested by the millions of images created with PicsArt’s existing consumer business. Choose from pre-created workflow templates to combine PicsArt’s APIs across images and apps. 3. Gemini What it does best: Gemini’s API adds intelligence to your image production workflow. Rather than focusing on pixel-level edits, it analyzes images, applies reasoning, and generates structured guidance that other tools can execute. For visual production workflows, Gemini is best at assessing image sets against brand and marketplace standards. Ideal use case: You’re the marketing lead for an e‑commerce company with photo-production teams across the globe. Use Gemini to unify inconsistent or non-compliant product imagery. Gemini can verify background color, detect required angles, check logo placement compliance, and route images through your editing tools before final approval. The tool isn’t specialized in e‑commerce, so for the best results, make sure to provide it with the specific standards or instructions, and double check results against marketplace or brand guidelines. Pros: Adds a reasoning layer to your existing editing stack, eliminating the need for manual review. Helps enforce consistent brand and compliance standards across large SKU catalogs. Generates structured guidance that integrates with image processors, DAM systems, and marketplace workflows. Note: Gemini excels at generating and editing individual images. For end-to-end production workflows where every output must look identical, a workflow-focused API is a better fit. Learn more: Photoroom vs Nano Banana Pro comparison: a model vs a complete AI product 4. Remove.bg What it does best: Remove.bg API was trained and created for a single purpose: removing and replacing image backgrounds. The tool also allows you to customize position, crop margins, scale, and output. Ideal use case: You’re launching your product line on Amazon and need to adapt current and future photography to its marketplace standards. Instead of shooting new product photography with white backgrounds, use Remove.bg ’s API to remove and replace existing backgrounds, center products in frame, and scale the product in relation to the image size. Pros: Integrate Remove.bg into any system with API access, including e‑commerce platforms, DAM/PIM, CMS, and internal tools. Create automatic workflows through integrations with Zapier and Make. Easy to configure, with fewer variables than more complex APIs and less room for human error. 5. Jasper What it does best: Jasper is an AI-powered platform designed to create and execute marketing-focused workflows. In 2025, they acquired Clipdrop, an image editing API. Together, they integrate brand and company knowledge with AI-powered tools to refine imagery and generate associated assets, like alt text. Ideal use case: You run the Shopify store for a small-batch perfume company. Add Jasper’s image editing API to your content management system to automatically clean up product photos (remove backgrounds, adjust lighting, reconfigure composition), align them with brand standards, and prepare them for upload. Pros: Can be combined with Jasper’s other AI-powered tools, like caption generation, for end-to-end marketing workflows. Default and user-designed templates allow you to create custom workflows by combining multiple API calls. 6. Claid AI What it does best: Claid AI's Image Editing API automates photo optimization and processing at scale. The API focuses on enhancement-first workflows and is best for enterprise technical or operations teams working with large batches of imagery. Ideal use case: You run operations for a global real estate company, managing the team and workflows responsible for placing employee headshots on the company website and in external realtor databases. Instead of requiring remote employees to follow strict guidelines or editing each image one by one, use Claid to automatically remove the background, improve lighting, and upscale photo resolution for each headshot as it’s uploaded. Pros: Combine multiple operations in a single API request. (Note: There are limitations to the tools that can be automatically combined in a single workflow.) Process images asynchronously with batch operations—ideal for handling large-scale image uploads without blocking workflows. Category-specific AI models are trained separately for products, cars, and general imagery. Learn more: Photoroom vs Claid comparison: e‑commerce visual tools 7. Open AI What it does best: OpenAI specializes in AI-powered prompt-based image editing, allowing you to reuse a single image multiple times through creative repurposing. Ideal use case: You lead marketing campaigns for a specialty foods store, and need seasonal campaign variations or marketplace-specific adaptations for all of your products. Instead of scheduling photoshoots for every seasonal theme or promotional campaign, use OpenAI's API to generate dozens of product image variations from one photo with simple text prompts. OpenAI is a general-use tool and doesn’t always generate e‑commerce ready results; take advantage of its chat feature to make adjustments. Pros: Process up to 16 input images simultaneously for complex multi-product compositions and batch edits in a single API call. Use natural language prompts up to 32,000 characters with GPT Image models, allowing detailed editing instructions without learning technical parameters or design software. How to choose the right image editing API If you need one task (e.g., background removal) Single-purpose image APIs are designed to reliably and consistently make one edit across hundreds or thousands of images at once. Look for an API that focuses on the features you need and can be integrated into existing content management programs. If you can find a free trial, make sure that the tool works consistently across image subjects. If you need creative edits inside an app Look for a creative editing API that allows you to adapt AI-powered editing tools, templates, and other features into an existing app. Some APIs integrate with existing photo editing tools, such as Photoshop, or can be used in your own app for consumer-facing workflows. The API and app should work together to streamline existing workflows, including the ability to export images in platform-specific sizes and according to platform standards. If you need scalable product visuals Scalable product visuals require end-to-end workflows that encompass each part of the image editing process. Look for tools that allow you to combine and customize workflows for your e‑commerce store’s unique brand standards and needs at a high volume — think thousands of images at once. Outputs should also be production-ready; this doesn’t just mean consistent and high quality, your API should be able to deliver these images exactly where they need to go in your tech stack. Among all the best image editing APIs, Photoroom’s API stands out for its ability to deliver production ready visuals at scale. If you need AI reasoning over images Look for a tool that offers advanced AI capabilities, can understand the nuances of a particular photoset, and generate outcomes based on that context. You want an image editing API that can distinguish between a car, a shoe, and a hamburger and assess the correct action for each without additional instruction. Common mistakes when choosing an image editing API Optimizing for model quality instead of workflow Teams often choose the API with the most accurate background removal or the highest-quality upscaling based on benchmark tests, only to discover it doesn't fit their actual production needs. The best API matches your speed requirements and integration architecture, not just demo quality. Treating editing as a one-off action Most workflows require multiple sequential edits, so choosing an API based on a single operation (e.g., "Can it remove backgrounds?") doesn’t allow you to evaluate the tool against your complete needs. Instead, create a list of your most frequent and reused edits, and look for a tool that can handle them and associated operations in a single system. Ignoring format and aspect-ratio reuse Most teams need multiple versions of the same image for different channels and marketplaces. Without intelligent cropping controls or outpainting capabilities, you'll process the same images repeatedly for each new dimension. This oversight can skyrocket API costs and processing time when adapting content across platforms. Confusing creative generation with production editing Generating new creative assets requires different capabilities than optimizing existing photography. Generation-focused tools handle creative ideation well but are often not fast or consistent enough for removing backgrounds, resizing, and rescaling. At the same time, most (but not all) production-optimized tools excel at high-volume catalog work but struggle with creative variations. Understand which workflow you're building before selecting an image editing API. Choosing APIs that cannot scale predictably The core benefit of an image editing API is the ability to scale production workflows, whether you’re creating an end-to-end process or repeating a single editing task across 1,000 images. APIs that can’t reliably provide consistent outputs interrupt workflows instead of improving them. Choose the right image editing API for your workflow There is no universal “best” image editing API — what’s best for your business will depend on your workflow: what you produce, how often you create or edit images, and where they go next, like catalogs, social media, or marketplaces. The right tool will automate a meaningful part of your visual production workflow, shifting your team’s focus from single, manual edits to high-speed image refinement and automatic placement. Photoroom is the full AI visual solution for e‑commerce, with a flexible model and AI-powered tools for end-to-end visual production. It's not just the tools (like background removal, AI Shadows, or aspect ratio reuse) but the customizable and scalable workflows. Photoroom's API lets you combine tools into a custom editing pipeline: whether you’re transforming studio photography into lifestyle imagery or making product photos compliant with marketplace standards. And its reliable, tested AI model delivers fast, consistent outputs across thousands of images at once. Download Photoroom from the App Store or Google Play , or use the web app to get started.

title: Apollo vs. Lusha: Which should you choose in 2026?
summary: An honest, buyer-scenario comparison of Apollo and Lusha in 2026, with published pricing, data scale, and clear guidance on which fits your team.
body_text: Apollo is the better fit if you want an all-in-one prospecting platform where the database, sequencing, and dialer live in one place at a low per-seat price. Lusha is the better fit if you mainly need accurate direct dials and verified emails inside a lightweight extension, with strong compliance credentials and no sequencing overhead. Apollo vs. Lusha at a glance Apollo Lusha Category All-in-one prospecting platform Contact-data provider / extension Best for Teams that want data plus outreach in one seat Teams that need accurate dials and emails only Standout capability Combined database, sequencing, and dialer Verified mobile numbers, privacy compliance Data scale Over 230M contacts (vendor figure) Over 300M contacts and over 30M companies (vendor figure) Published pricing Free to about $119/user/month Free; Pro ~$29 to $52 and Premium ~$300/user/month (credit slider); custom Scale Compliance notes SOC 2, GDPR, CCPA (per its site) ISO 27701, SOC 2, GDPR, CCPA (per its site) What is the core difference between Apollo and Lusha? Apollo is a platform; Lusha is a data source. This single distinction drives every other decision. Apollo bundles a contact database with sequencing, a dialer, deal management, and assistive AI, so a rep can find an account, load it into a cadence, and start emailing and calling without leaving the tool. Apollo is used by more than 600,000 companies and reported roughly $200M in ARR, and it acquired the buyer-intent and product-signal company Pocus in March 2026 to deepen its signals layer. Lusha does one job and aims to do it cleanly: return a verified email and, more importantly, a direct dial or mobile number for the person in front of you, usually through a browser extension that overlays company sites, social profiles, and your CRM. There is no cadence engine and no dialer. You take the data and act on it elsewhere. Which has better B2B data, Apollo or Lusha? It depends on whether you value breadth or verified reach. Apollo wins on raw coverage; Lusha competes on the accuracy of the hardest field to verify, the mobile number. Apollo claims a database of over 230M contacts (a vendor figure), which makes it one of the largest self-serve databases at its price point. This breadth is why many teams treat Apollo as a low-cost data layer even when they run outreach elsewhere. For how Apollo compares with other data-first tools, see Clay vs. Apollo and Seamless vs. Apollo . Lusha does not try to out-scale Apollo. Its pitch is that the records it returns, especially cell phone numbers, are more likely to connect, and that its data practices are auditable. Lusha markets verified mobile coverage and holds ISO 27701, the privacy-information-management standard, on top of GDPR and CCPA compliance. For teams whose outbound leans on phone connects, or who face procurement scrutiny on data sourcing, this posture matters more than the size of the index. For a like-for-like on data providers, see Cognism vs. Lusha . If you want a deeper look at how the major providers stack up on coverage and verification, see our guide to the best B2B data providers . How do Apollo and Lusha compare on price in 2026? Apollo is priced to convert individual reps and small teams. Its published tiers run from a free plan up to about $119/user/month for its higher self-serve tier, per its pricing page, with credits that govern exports and enrichment. This low entry point, paired with the bundled sequencer and dialer, is Apollo's central value argument. Lusha also publishes a free plan and paid tiers (Pro reported around $29 to $52 and Premium now around $300/user/month on a credit slider), with a custom Scale plan for larger teams, per its pricing page. Because Lusha sells credits for contact reveals rather than a full outreach platform, you are paying for data access, not for a place to run campaigns. On the lower Pro tier the two are close on data alone, but Lusha's Premium climbs steeply, and the gap widens further once you factor in that Apollo's price also buys you the sequencer and dialer. Both reward discipline. Reveal only the contacts you will actually work, or the per-record cost climbs. Which is easier to deploy and use day to day? Lusha is the faster thing to switch on; Apollo is the more capable thing to live in. Lusha's extension installs in minutes and starts returning data on the pages your reps already visit. There is very little to configure because there is very little surface area. This is the point. Apollo asks for more setup because it does more: mailbox connection, sequence building, CRM sync, dialer configuration. Reviewers report that Apollo's breadth can feel busy, and that data accuracy varies by segment and region. The payoff is that once it is configured, a rep works the whole motion from one screen. If your team already lives in a separate sequencer or CRM, Apollo's platform depth is partly redundant, and Lusha's narrow focus is the cleaner add. For how Apollo's built-in outreach stacks up against a dedicated sequencer, see Apollo vs. Outreach . When should you pick something else entirely? When the job you actually want done is the outreach, not the lookup. The shared limitation is easy to miss: both Apollo and Lusha are data tools. Each hands you contacts and leaves the sending, calling, and replying to your reps. This is the right model if you have people to run it. If you would rather the prospecting motion ran itself, an autonomous platform like Artisan is a third path. It pairs a 250M-contact business-to-business database with an AI business development representative (BDR), Ava, who finds the leads, writes and sends the outreach, handles replies, and books meetings, so the data and the activation live in one system rather than two tools plus the humans in between, on usage-based pricing sized to lead volume rather than a seat per rep. See how this works on the AI sales agent page. For a direct comparison, see Artisan vs. Apollo . This is a different purchase from either tool here. If you specifically want a database and a browser extension, Apollo and Lusha remain the relevant comparison. For broader roundups, see the best Apollo alternatives and the best Lusha alternatives . Choose Apollo if... You want data, sequencing, and a dialer in one low-cost seat rather than a stack. You are a startup or SMB team standardizing your whole outbound motion on a single tool. Broad contact coverage at an accessible price matters more than best-in-class mobile accuracy. You want buyer and product signals in the same platform (post-Pocus). Choose Lusha if... You mainly need accurate direct dials and verified emails, fed into a stack you already run. Phone connect rates are central to your outbound and mobile accuracy is the priority. Procurement or legal cares about data sourcing and privacy certifications (ISO 27701). You want a lightweight extension with minimal setup, not another platform to configure. Frequently asked questions Is Apollo or Lusha better for a startup? For most startups standardizing on one tool, Apollo is the stronger single purchase because its tiers, from free to about $119/user/month, include sequencing and a dialer alongside the database. Lusha is the better pick when the startup already runs a separate sequencer or CRM and only needs a clean, compliant source of dials and emails to feed it. Which has more accurate phone numbers, Apollo or Lusha? Lusha positions accuracy of direct dials and mobile numbers as its core differentiator, backed by verification claims and ISO 27701 privacy certification. Apollo offers phone data too, but reviewers report accuracy varies by region and segment. If phone connects drive your pipeline, test both on your own target list before committing, since accuracy is territory-dependent for every provider. Can Apollo replace Lusha? For many teams, yes: Apollo includes contact data, so a team using Lusha purely for emails and dials could consolidate into Apollo. The case for keeping Lusha is data quality on mobile numbers and its privacy certifications. Teams that live or die by phone connects sometimes run both, using Lusha to verify the numbers that matter most. Does either tool run outreach for you? No. Both are prospecting and data tools. Apollo gives you a sequencer and dialer to run outreach yourself; Lusha gives you data to run outreach elsewhere. Neither writes and sends campaigns or handles replies autonomously. This autonomous model is a separate category of tool, covered in our guide to the AI BDR . Is there an alternative to both Apollo and Lusha? Yes. Both are data tools that leave you to run the outreach; if you would rather the whole motion ran itself, an autonomous platform is the alternative. Artisan pairs its own contact database with an AI BDR, Ava, who sources, writes, sends, and works replies end to end on usage-based pricing , so you are not buying a database plus an extension and then supplying the people to act on them. See Artisan's AI sales agent for how it differs. How much do Apollo and Lusha cost? Apollo publishes tiers from free to about $119/user/month, per its pricing page, with credits for exports and enrichment. Lusha publishes a free plan plus Pro and Premium tiers (reported around $29 to $52 and around $300/user/month respectively, on a credit slider) and a custom Scale plan, per its pricing page. Both use credit models, so real cost depends on how many contacts you reveal each month. Is Lusha GDPR compliant? Lusha markets GDPR and CCPA compliance and holds ISO 27701, the international standard for privacy information management, which is part of why it appeals to teams under procurement scrutiny. As with any data provider, compliant use also depends on how your team handles and stores the data, so confirm your own processes alongside the vendor's certifications. Which should a phone-heavy outbound team choose? Lusha, in most cases, if you already run a dialer elsewhere and just need the best mobile numbers to feed it. Apollo, if you want the dialer, the data, and the sequencer in one seat and can accept region-variable phone accuracy. Test connect rates on your real territory first; this number decides it more than any feature list. The bottom line Apollo and Lusha solve overlapping problems at different depths. Apollo is a full prospecting platform that happens to include a large database; Lusha is a focused, compliance-forward data source that happens to be very easy to deploy. Pick Apollo to run your motion from one tool at a low seat price. Pick Lusha to feed accurate, auditable contacts into a stack you already trust. title: Salario mínimo en Colombia 2026: cuánto es y cómo quedó
summary: Salario mínimo en Colombia 2026: $1.750.905 (+23%) más auxilio de transporte de $249.095. Conoce el ingreso total, el decreto y su impacto.
body_text: El salario mínimo en Colombia 2026 subió a 1.750.905 pesos mensuales, un aumento del 23 por ciento, uno de los más altos de la región. Pero el número por sí solo no cuenta toda la historia: lo que define el bienestar del trabajador es cuánto rinde ese ingreso frente a la inflación y cómo, cuándo y en qué moneda recibe su pago. En esta guía verás el salario mínimo mensual legal vigente (SMMLV) para 2026, el auxilio de transporte, el ingreso total, quién lo decreta y su impacto. Ontop es una plataforma global de nómina y pagos que permite a las empresas contratar y pagar equipos en más de 150 países, y a los trabajadores recibir su dinero en dólares sin fricción. Puntos clave El SMMLV para 2026 es de 1.750.905 pesos mensuales , un aumento del 23 por ciento frente a 2025, según los Decretos 1469 y 1470 de 2025. El auxilio de transporte sube a 249.095 pesos (un 24.5 por ciento más), para un ingreso total de alrededor de 2.000.000 de pesos . Los decretos se expidieron el 29 de diciembre de 2025 y rigen desde el 1 de enero de 2026. El aumento superó la propuesta empresarial (7.21 por ciento) y la sindical (16 por ciento), con el IPC de 2025 certificado por el DANE en 5.10 por ciento. Los trabajadores remotos que cobran del extranjero suelen superar el mínimo local; lo decisivo es el método y la moneda del pago. Las empresas que contratan en Colombia deben pagar al menos el mínimo más el auxilio de transporte cuando aplica, y cumplir las obligaciones laborales. ¿Cuál es el salario mínimo en Colombia en 2026? El salario mínimo mensual legal vigente (SMMLV) en Colombia para 2026 es de 1.750.905 pesos, un incremento del 23 por ciento frente a 2025. A esto se suma un auxilio de transporte de 249.095 pesos para quienes ganan hasta dos salarios mínimos, lo que eleva el ingreso total a cerca de 2.000.000 de pesos. Las cifras rigen desde el 1 de enero de 2026. El aumento se oficializó mediante los Decretos 1469 y 1470 de 2025, expedidos el 29 de diciembre de 2025. El Gobierno decretó el ajuste por decreto tras no alcanzarse un acuerdo entre empleadores y centrales sindicales. Concepto 2025 2026 Var. Salario mínimo (SMMLV) $1.423.500 $1.750.905 +23% Auxilio de transporte $200.000 $249.095 +24.5% Ingreso total mensual $1.623.500 ~$2.000.000 +23% ¿Quién define el salario mínimo y cómo se calcula? En Colombia el salario mínimo se fija cada año mediante concertación en la Comisión Permanente de Concertación de Políticas Salariales y Laborales, integrada por gobierno, empleadores y trabajadores. Cuando no hay acuerdo, el Gobierno lo define por decreto, considerando la inflación del año (IPC), la productividad y el crecimiento económico. Para 2026, el sector empresarial proponía un 7.21 por ciento y las centrales sindicales un 16 por ciento. El Gobierno decretó finalmente un 23 por ciento, apoyándose en el concepto de salario vital, mientras el IPC de 2025 fue certificado por el DANE en 5.10 por ciento. Es decir, el aumento superó con amplitud la inflación del año. ¿Cuál es el impacto del salario mínimo en Colombia? Un aumento del 23 por ciento tiene un impacto doble. Para el trabajador, mejora el ingreso disponible y el poder de compra, sobre todo en los hogares de menores ingresos. Para la economía, impulsa el consumo interno, aunque genera debate sobre la presión en costos laborales, la formalidad y la inflación futura, en especial para las pequeñas y medianas empresas. Quienes respaldan el ajuste destacan la recuperación del poder adquisitivo. Quienes advierten riesgos señalan que un aumento muy por encima del IPC puede encarecer la contratación formal y trasladarse a precios. En la práctica, para el trabajador el número importa, pero también importa la puntualidad del pago y la moneda en la que lo recibe. ¿Cómo afecta el salario mínimo a los trabajadores remotos y freelancers? Para los trabajadores remotos colombianos, el salario mínimo local suele ser solo una referencia. Muchos cobran de empresas en el extranjero por montos superiores al mínimo nacional, así que el reto no es cuánto ganan, sino cómo reciben ese dinero sin perder valor. Cuando un freelancer cobra en dólares y su plataforma aplica una conversión forzada a pesos con un tipo de cambio desfavorable, parte del ingreso se evapora en el spread. Lo mismo pasa con pagos lentos o comisiones ocultas. Por eso conviene recibir y mantener el dinero en dólares y decidir cuándo convertirlo. Con una cuenta global en dólares el trabajador controla su saldo. Para profundizar, revisa cómo cobrar en dólares desde Latinoamérica . ¿Cómo pueden las empresas pagar en Colombia cumpliendo la ley? Las empresas que contratan en Colombia deben pagar al menos el SMMLV, sumar el auxilio de transporte cuando corresponde y cumplir con la seguridad social y las obligaciones laborales. Para una compañía extranjera sin entidad en el país, hacerlo por cuenta propia implica trámites y riesgo de incumplimiento. Ontop es una plataforma global de nómina y pagos que permite contratar y pagar talento en Colombia cumpliendo con la normativa local, sin abrir una entidad. La plataforma gestiona la nómina, los pagos y el cumplimiento, para que la empresa se enfoque en el trabajo y el profesional reciba su pago a tiempo. Preguntas frecuentes ¿Cuánto es el salario mínimo en Colombia en 2026? Rige desde el 1 de enero de 2026. ¿Cuánto aumentó el salario mínimo en 2026? Aumentó un 23 por ciento frente a 2025, muy por encima del IPC de 2025 (5.10 por ciento según el DANE), según los Decretos 1469 y 1470 de 2025. ¿El auxilio de transporte se suma al salario mínimo? Sí. El auxilio de transporte de 249.095 pesos aplica para quienes ganan hasta dos salarios mínimos y se suma al salario para efectos de ingreso mensual. ¿Los trabajadores remotos ganan el salario mínimo? No necesariamente. Muchos cobran de empresas extranjeras por montos superiores al mínimo local; lo relevante es el método, la moneda y la puntualidad del pago. Reflexiones finales El salario mínimo en Colombia 2026 marca uno de los mayores aumentos recientes, con 1.750.905 pesos más auxilio de transporte.
